channel.title: The Brief — Adam's News
channel.description: Every story from Adam's three daily briefs (9 AM / 5 PM / 10 PM CT) as its own item, readable right in your feed reader, with a link to the original article.

item.title: Ukraine fires nearly 1,200 drones at Russia in its biggest barrage in years — as the peace talks widen to Europe, and Europe pushes back
item.description:
Ukraine launched one of its biggest aerial attacks of the war overnight, firing almost 1,200 drones at targets across Russia, while Russia hit Ukraine with 117 drones of its own — including a strike that set a Kyiv hospital on fire and one that wounded 25 people in Zaporizhzhia. The exchange came as US envoys tried to widen the peace talks to include Europe, and European leaders pushed back hard against Moscow's attempt to put the post-Cold War security order itself on the table.
The details are stark on both sides. Russia's Defense Ministry said its air defences downed 1,198 Ukrainian long-range drones between late Thursday and early Friday, across more than 15 regions — but strikes still got through in three regions, killing seven people including a 12-year-old and wounding 17, according to local officials. Moscow's mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, said 467 drones targeted the capital overnight. In Volgograd, in southern Russia, drones hit an industrial area, killing four people and injuring two, regional governor Andrei Bocharov said; the city is home to a major Lukoil refinery, and unverified video on social media purported to show it on fire, though there was no official confirmation the refinery was hit. Ukraine has concentrated its long-range strikes this year on Russian oil infrastructure, aiming to cut the energy earnings funding Moscow's invasion.
Russia's reply was smaller but hit civilians. Ukraine's Air Force said it shot down 80 of 117 Russian drones launched overnight. In Kyiv, a Russian drone struck the Institute of Traumatology and Orthopedics in the Shevchenkivskyi district at about 3 a.m. local time, setting it on fire and badly damaging it while patients and medical staff were inside; one person was injured. Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi said Russian forces targeted energy infrastructure — mainly high-voltage substations — in nine regions, with damage also to a logistics terminal in Kharkiv and a dormitory in Rivne. In Odesa, two people were killed and five wounded; in Zaporizhzhia, a 17-year-old boy was killed and a single strike on two five-storey apartment blocks wounded 25 people, including six children. First Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov said the attacks caused widespread power outages across about half of the country's regions.
What each side is arguing about now is bigger than the battlefield. After two days of talks in Abu Dhabi, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner briefed Putin in Moscow on Thursday, then Zelenskyy in Dublin, where European leaders were meeting. Kushner said late Thursday that Russia had agreed to include Europe in the next round of talks, writing that "we cannot conclude this deal without the Europeans being at the table" — a reversal of Moscow's long insistence that European governments be excluded. But on Friday afternoon the Kremlin said it had not yet agreed: spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow would decide on an expanded format only "once we understand their real intentions and their willingness to contribute to the peace process." European leaders, meanwhile, are alarmed at what Moscow wants to discuss. Unconfirmed reports say Russia has demanded wider European security concessions, including Finland leaving NATO and a pledge not to base troops in the Baltics. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz rejected the premise outright: "Russia wants to talk about questions of European security architecture. We don't need to talk about that. There is one," he said, referring to NATO. The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said Europe must insist on a ceasefire before taking the negotiations further — the opposite of what Putin demands — warning that "if we start to talk about what Russia is asking regarding the security architecture, we actually walk into the traps that Russia is setting us." The Institute for the Study of War assessed late Thursday that Moscow is aiming "to dismantle NATO and the post-Cold War European security architecture."
For ordinary people the war's grind is now measured in power cuts and hospital evacuations. Russia has battered Ukraine's power grid every winter since the invasion began, and Friday's outages hit about half the country's regions as temperatures drop. In Kyiv, a hospital treating civilians caught fire in the middle of the night; in Zaporizhzhia, families in two apartment blocks were wounded, six of them children. On the Russian side, four workers died in Volgograd's industrial zone. Zelenskyy also repeated his complaint on Friday about speed limits on the US Starshield system — SpaceX's military-grade Starlink — which he says caps Ukrainian drones at 161 km/h (100 mph) across the front line, making it impossible to intercept Russia's fast jet-powered drones. SpaceX told CNN there had been no change in service, and the White House and Pentagon have not responded.
In short: Ukraine answered the diplomatic push with its largest drone barrage in years, Russia answered with strikes on hospitals, homes and power stations, and the talks themselves are now stuck on a new fight — whether Europe gets a seat, and whether Moscow gets to renegotiate the security order that has held since the Cold War. Watch the Dublin summit's decision on a European envoy, and whether the next round of talks gets a date.
Sources:
Source: europesays.com.

item.title: Iran hands Washington a seven-day roadmap to end the war — and Trump says he doesn't need a deal
item.description:
Iran formally submitted a seven-day roadmap to end its war with the United States, its foreign minister said on Friday — and within hours, President Donald Trump appeared to reject it, saying the US "doesn't need a deal with Iran" and redirecting Vice President JD Vance away from the diplomacy entirely. The whiplash came a day after US and Iranian forces exchanged fire in the Strait of Hormuz, in the sharpest direct clash there in this round of the war.
The details of Tehran's offer, as laid out by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi to reporters outside the UN Security Council on Friday, are specific: the plan was conveyed to Washington through Qatar, and the seven-day clock would start as soon as the US accepts it. The first steps would take four to five days, the Strait of Hormuz would reopen on the sixth day, and on day seven, talks with the US would begin on a final deal covering Iran's nuclear programme. In return, Al Jazeera reports, Washington would lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, release an estimated $12 billion in frozen Iranian assets, and observe a ceasefire covering the region, including Lebanon and Yemen. "The choice now rests with the United States," Araghchi said, adding that "if there is seriousness on the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared."
What Washington is saying, though, points the other way. The Wall Street Journal reported later on Friday that Trump had rejected Iran's proposal, and that he is "privately sceptical" Iran would meet his demands, telling aides he expects a renewed bombing campaign after the November midterm elections. On Thursday, Trump wrote on social media: "We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We've got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we've got their Strait!" — and he directed Vance, who has played a central role in the diplomacy, to focus "his complete and total attention" on alleged crime and corruption in Democratic-run cities and states. The directive came a day after the Journal reported Vance was considering face-to-face peace talks with a hard-line Iranian security official. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called Iran's demands "absurd" on Tuesday, citing in particular the demand for reparations for the war. Analysts quoted by Al Jazeera were sceptical the roadmap changes anything: "Basically nothing has really changed," said Cyrus Schayegh of the Geneva Graduate Institute, arguing Iran wants to keep the leverage it gained during the war while Washington resists returning to the June framework — a memorandum of understanding brokered by Qatar and Pakistan that collapsed within weeks.
The shooting, meanwhile, has not stopped. US Central Command said it launched strikes on Iran on Thursday after three US Navy guided-missile destroyers came under attack from Iranian missiles, drones and small boats in the strait. Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters accused the US of violating the ceasefire by attacking an Iranian oil tanker and another vessel, and of targeting civilian areas including Qeshm Island. Trump on Thursday appeared to downplay the clash, saying the ceasefire remained in effect, while Iran's state-run Press TV said the situation had gone "back to normal." The exchange followed Iran's military saying four oil tankers were hit by explosions in the strait after ignoring warnings — a claim Reuters said it could not independently verify.
For ordinary people the cost keeps compounding at the pump and the checkout. Brent crude settled Thursday at $95.82 a barrel, up $3.06 or 3.3%, and WTI closed at $88.74, up $2.21 — after the Houthi claims against Saudi energy sites and the strait incidents — though both benchmarks were still down about 2.5% for the week and eased slightly on Friday morning, with Brent around $95.50. US gasoline averaged $3.98 a gallon and diesel $6.16 on November 10, roughly 30% and 65% above a year earlier, according to AAA. Shipping through the strait has been at a near standstill since late February, and Brent is up about 40% compared with before the war.
In short: Tehran put a concrete, dated offer on the table — blockade lifted, $12 billion released, Hormuz open in six days — and Trump answered that America doesn't need a deal at all, pulling his vice president off the file. The one thing both sides agree on is that the shooting continues: US destroyers and Iranian forces traded fire in the strait on Thursday. Watch whether the White House formally responds to the roadmap, and whether the post-midterm bombing campaign Trump reportedly expects actually materialises.
Sources:
Source: aljazeeranews-mggx1uo47w.edgeone.app.

item.title: No new Houthi attacks overnight — but Pakistan condemned the strikes at the UN and Saudi Arabia talked to China
item.description:
No new Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia were reported overnight.
The fallout from Thursday's claimed strikes continued instead: Pakistan's ambassador to the UN, Syed Haider Shah, condemned the Houthi attacks "in the strongest terms" at the Security Council after members renewed the Yemen sanctions, calling for an immediate and unconditional end to them. And Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan met China's special envoy for Middle East affairs, Zhai Jun, in Riyadh to discuss the Houthi attacks and diplomatic efforts to prevent further escalation.
The Houthis' Thursday claims — a drone and a ballistic missile at East-West Pipeline pumping station 7, about 330 km west of Riyadh, plus strikes on Yanbu, an Aramco facility in Riyadh, a cargo plane at Sharurah airport and Khamis Mushait airbase — remain unconfirmed by Riyadh, and the coalition says it intercepted two drones on Thursday. (Daily The Destination · Suryaa Now · Demócrata)
Source: dailythedestination.com.

item.title: Nvidia: the interim CEO is the CFO who pushed back on Huang's bets
item.description:
Reuters profiled Colette Kress, the 59-year-old CFO who took over as Nvidia's interim CEO after Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday.
Kress, CFO since September 2013, spent years as the one Nvidia executive willing to check Huang's enormous, often risky ambitions, pushing back as he drove the chipmaker deeper into multibillion-dollar AI investments, according to two people familiar with the matter. She keeps the CFO job while running the company, and whether she keeps the CEO role permanently is undecided — Nvidia executive Ian Buck, who helped launch AI on Nvidia chips and led development of CUDA, is among the names surfacing as a successor.
The board has started looking at internal and external candidates with no set timeline. The next real test is earnings on Tuesday, November 17.
(Reuters via WNFL Sports · Technology.org)
Source: wnflsports.com.

item.title: KEV watch — no new additions; the Barracuda pair and an Ivanti flaw come due today
item.description:
No new CISA KEV additions were published overnight.
The federal patch deadline for the Barracuda pair (CVE-2026-116606, 9.3, and CVE-2026-111560, 8.6) falls today, November 13, along with Ivanti Connect Secure CVE-2026-118527 (4.3, predictable identifiers in the chain behind the exploited login bypass). The six added November 10 — including the Chrome zero-day CVE-2026-125350 and the Outlook zero-day CVE-2026-124194 — are due November 24.
The catalog stands at 1,779 entries. A weekly roundup notes CISA added 11 exploited flaws this week in total, including two zero-days, spanning Barracuda, Microsoft Outlook, Chrome, Cisco BroadWorks, Openwave, OpenSSH (SSHole), GPUStack, IBM Aspera, SonicWall and SignalWire — all previously reported in this brief's earlier editions.
(ImmunitySec KEV · Medium/Loginsoft weekly KEV roundup)
Source: immunitysec.com.

item.title: meta/astryx
item.description:
is still the fastest-growing repo, up about 1,800 stars in a day to ~26.7k — Meta's open design system for React. storytold/craft-anything passed 30.9k stars, still gaining about 1,620 a day.
New risers: apex-compute/ANR (Apex Neural Rendering, C++, +847/day) and agentes-chat/agentes-chat (+521/day) — an open-source, self-hosted Slack alternative where your team and AI agents work together in channels and DMs, with agents running on Claude, ChatGPT/Codex, Gemini or Grok, MCP tools, and their own computer and browser. GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src (+739/day) and openai/codex-security (+643/day) keep climbing, and we-promise/sure, the self-hosted personal finance app, gained 967 stars in a day.
REA kept climbing at about +2,100/day to ~456k. (Daily Diff · Trendar · GitDiscover)
Source: github-trending-dev.vercel.app.

item.title: Murdaugh retrial: dismissal hearing is today in Lexington
item.description:
Alex Murdaugh's lawyers are in court this morning in Lexington, South Carolina, asking Judge Debra McCaslin to throw out the original murder indictments for the 2021 killings of his wife and son.
The defence argues lead SLED agent David Owen misled the July 2022 grand jury, telling it the spatter on Murdaugh's shirt held Maggie and Paul's DNA eight months after the state's own lab reported no human blood on it. Even if McCaslin grants the long-shot request, it likely won't stop the April 5, 2027 retrial — prosecutors can seek fresh indictments from the Colleton County grand jury, which next sits December 10, and the defence says it won't oppose that.
Murdaugh's 2023 convictions and life sentences were thrown out by the South Carolina Supreme Court in May after a court clerk was found to have improperly influenced jurors. (AP via HeadlinesXtra · DeWitt Substack)
Source: headlinesxtra.com.

item.title: Houthis claim new strikes on Saudi oil and airports as the UN extends sanctions and oil jumps $3
item.description:
The Houthis widened their campaign against Saudi Arabia on Thursday, claiming drone strikes on a pumping station on the East-West oil pipeline, the Yanbu oil facility on the Red Sea, and an Aramco facility in Riyadh — and on the ground in Yemen they captured two towns in a push to cut the road to Aden. The UN Security Council answered the same day by unanimously extending its Yemen sanctions for another year, and oil prices closed up $3 a barrel as the attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure escalated.
The details, as far as they can be verified, split between what the Houthis claim and what anyone else can confirm. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on Thursday that the group had hit a pumping station on the East-West Pipeline with a drone, struck the Yanbu oil facility, and targeted an Aramco facility in Riyadh, a military cargo plane at Sharurah airport near the Yemeni border, and the Khamis Mushait airbase — where he claimed a ballistic missile "scored a direct hit." Reuters reports the pipeline and Yanbu claims, and notes Saudi Arabia did not immediately respond to a request for comment, while the Houthis did not say which day the attacks were carried out. The Saudi-led coalition said separately that its air defences intercepted suspected Houthi drones over the Riyadh region and the Eastern Province on Thursday. The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) says it cannot verify the Houthis' claims, and notes the group has hit the East-West Pipeline before — a September attack forced Saudi authorities to close it for about 11 days of emergency repairs.
The ground war moved too. ISW reports the Houthis launched a combined-arms offensive in southeastern Lahij Governorate on November 11, opening with ballistic missile salvos on government staging areas at Ras al Arah and Kharaz and a strike on the government command headquarters in Aden City, then advancing on foot and in vehicles toward al Shatt and al Sarih. Government-aligned forces repelled the first push, but the Houthis captured al Shatt and the al Sarih junction on November 12, and Saudi-Yemeni government airstrikes on Houthi positions in al Shatt later that day indicate the Houthis still hold the town. ISW assesses the aim is to capture the high ground at Jabal Kharaz and cut the Mokha–Aden road, which would isolate government forces on the Red Sea coastal plain — including the units best able to defend Aden City. The Houthis also fired two ballistic missiles at government staging areas in Jawf and Marib governorates on Thursday, according to ISW, as government forces advance toward the town of al Hazm.
What each side is saying is now a straight contradiction on the shipping front as well. Iran's Revolutionary Guards claim two more large oil tankers exploded and caught fire in the early hours of Thursday after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz, taking their claimed toll to four tankers on fire. But UKMTO — the maritime reporting body — has logged only one strike off Oman on Tuesday, plus two projectile attacks on tankers reported by ISW, including one that hit an engine room. Reuters says it cannot independently verify the Iranian reports, and ISW assesses the mine claims are likely meant to shake ship operators' confidence in US escort operations and push vessels into Iranian waters. Meanwhile the UN Security Council voted unanimously on Thursday to extend Yemen-related sanctions for one more year — asset freezes and travel bans — while demanding an end to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. The Houthis again denied targeting Mecca, after Saudi civil defence said debris from two intercepted ballistic missiles fell in the Mecca region on Wednesday.
For ordinary people the stakes run through fuel prices and the cost of everything shipped. The East-West Pipeline is Saudi Arabia's workaround for a closed Hormuz, carrying about 4 million barrels a day — roughly 4% of global supply — to Yanbu on the Red Sea. Oil rose $3 a barrel on Thursday on the attacks and the Hormuz disruption, and German shipping giant Hapag-Lloyd says the strait closure is already costing it about $60 million a week in fuel and insurance. The Houthi campaign has also kept Riyadh's King Khalid airport disrupted for days, and the US Embassy still requires special approval for government staff to use Saudi airports.
In short: the Houthis claim they hit the pipeline that lets Saudi oil bypass Hormuz, plus Yanbu, Riyadh and two airbases — none of it confirmed by Riyadh — while on the ground they took two towns in a push toward Aden, and the UN answered with another year of sanctions. The verified facts are the coalition intercepts, the sanctions vote, and oil up $3. Watch for a Saudi damage statement on the pipeline and any UKMTO confirmation of the tanker claims.
Sources:
Source: understandingwar.org.

item.title: US–Iran diplomacy: Trump says talks are progressing, Tehran says the strait stays shut until its seven conditions are met
item.description:
Donald Trump said on Thursday that US–Iran talks are progressing and a deal to end the war could be within reach, as Tehran says it is still reviewing a US proposal delivered through mediator Pakistan. At the same time, Iran's parliament speaker said the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until Washington meets seven Iranian conditions — and Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agreed to keep talking, after their top military officials met in Tehran.
The details, as reported by Al Jazeera, are that Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said the US proposal remains "under review" and Tehran will send its response to key mediator Pakistan once it has "finalised its views." Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, a key mediator between Iran, the US and Israel, said he was "hopeful" the current momentum would lead to peace. Trump, for his part, said the conflict "will be over quickly" as Washington pushes for a deal over Tehran's nuclear programme and the Hormuz blockade. But the other side of the table is digging in: parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said in an interview on Wednesday that Washington has not formally responded to Iran's own terms, that "the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened until those seven conditions are implemented," and that Iran has proposed reopening the strait six days after the US meets the demands, with negotiations on a final agreement starting the following day.
What each side wants is still far apart. The seven conditions, as named in Iranian officials' statements, include lifting US sanctions, releasing frozen Iranian assets, ending the naval blockade of Iranian ports, compensation for war damage, and a halt to fighting on all fronts, including Lebanon. Iran's Tasnim news agency separately denied reports that Tehran had offered to reopen the strait in exchange for the US lifting the blockade, calling them "a lie and fabrication." Meanwhile the regional track moved: Iran said it will continue discussions with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey after their top military officials met in Tehran on Monday — hosted by Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei and attended by Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin — focused on a regional non-aggression network, the US–Iran negotiations, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, the strait and the US blockade. A senior Pakistani official told Reuters that Munir, with Trump's blessing to pursue diplomacy, had presented Iran with a proposal meant to offer something to both Washington and Tehran, with the Mecca-pact states and Qatar as possible guarantors if accepted.
For ordinary people the cost of the standoff keeps compounding. Hapag-Lloyd says the Hormuz closure is costing it about $60 million a week in fuel and insurance as companies avoid the waterway, and oil jumped $3 a barrel on Thursday on the Saudi attacks. In Lebanon, the fighting continued despite the US-brokered ceasefire: Al Jazeera reported late Thursday that at least 14 people were killed in Israeli air strikes across southern Lebanon, including 13 security personnel in a strike on a government building in Nabatieh, and that the Israeli army said it had hit 40 Hezbollah sites in the past day.
In short: the diplomacy has momentum — a US proposal on the table in Tehran, a four-country regional track, and Trump sounding upbeat — but Iran's public price for reopening Hormuz is seven conditions Washington hasn't answered, and the shooting hasn't stopped in Lebanon or the strait. Watch for Tehran's formal response to the US proposal, expected via Pakistan.
Sources:
Source: aljazeeranews.edgeone.app.

item.title: Google and Samsung's AI glasses go on pre-order — from $395, on sale December 10
item.description:
Google and Samsung opened pre-orders on Thursday for their first Android XR smart glasses — called Intelligent Eyewear — with Warby Parker frames starting at $395 and Gentle Monster frames at $449 to $489. They go on sale December 10 in the United States and South Korea, with demos at more than 360 Warby Parker stores and seven Samsung Experience Stores.
The details: the glasses are display-free for now — no screen in the lens — and run on Qualcomm's Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 chip, weighing about 41 grams with a battery lasting up to nine hours and a charging case that recharges them up to seven times. A 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera, open-ear speakers and microphones feed Google's Gemini assistant, which you summon with "Hey Gemini" or a tap on the temple. Google says Gemini can identify what you're looking at, give turn-by-turn directions through Google Maps in your ear, translate speech in real time across more than 70 languages, and handle busywork like adding something you see to a grocery list or checking your calendar from an event poster. A feature called Guided Vision gives conversational audio descriptions for people who are blind or have low vision, and an Aira integration can stream the camera feed to a trained human visual interpreter. There are 30 frame variations across the two brands — Warby Parker's Alden, Reid and Wren styles, and six Gentle Monster designs — with prescription options for most frames. They work with Pixel 7 and newer, select Samsung Galaxy phones on One UI 9 or later, and iPhone 13 Pro and newer. Google says a version with displays built into the lenses is being tested by people outside the company but gave no date for it.
What each side is saying splits on privacy, which is the whole argument about camera glasses. Google and Samsung lead with it: camera visuals from Gemini on the glasses are not saved in Gemini History and aren't used to train AI models or target ads, bystanders' faces are automatically redacted before Gemini processes them, an indicator light shows when you're recording and the glasses stop recording if the light is covered, data on the glasses is encrypted, and every pair has an off switch so they work as regular glasses. Samsung says voice and video data isn't used to train AI models by default. The open question is whether buyers and bystanders trust that — Meta's Ray-Ban glasses have already normalised camera glasses in public, and Google is clearly trying to out-promise Meta on the privacy front rather than compete on it.
For ordinary people this is the first real test of whether Google's version of AI glasses is a product or a demo. At $395 with prescription options and demos in hundreds of stores, it's priced and sold like normal eyewear, not a developer kit — but only in the US and South Korea at launch, and only if you own a recent Pixel, Galaxy or iPhone. If it lands, it's Google's first consumer AI hardware with Gemini built in from the start.
In short: Google and Samsung's Gemini glasses are real, buyable from December 10 at $395 and up, with a heavy privacy pitch aimed at the bystander problem — but no display in the lens yet, and only two countries at launch. Watch whether the December 10 launch sells out or sits, and when the display version appears.
Sources:
Source: storage.googleapis.com.

item.title: Nvidia fallout: the board was reportedly preparing to oust Huang — over an alleged relationship with a woman said to be a Chinese spy
item.description:
New details emerged Thursday on why Jensen Huang resigned.
The Wall Street Journal reported the board was preparing to oust him on Wednesday night, and Reuters reported the stock had lost about $600 billion in market value since the board announced on Sunday it had opened an investigation into Huang's relationship with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. Nvidia's own release gives no reason for the resignation.
Trading volume hit 734.3 million shares on Thursday — 423% above the three-month average — as the stock fell as much as 14% to a 52-week low of $148.80 before closing down 4.34% at $166.19. Bernstein cut its price target in half, from $400 to $200.
Earnings stay on Tuesday, November 17 — the next real test of whether the company can steady itself without its co-founder. (CoinDesk · Motley Fool · FinanceFeeds)
Source: Www.coindesk.com.

item.title: N-able follow-up: no confirmed customer compromises yet — but a follow-up hotfix is still coming
item.description:
N-able says that as of November 12 there is no evidence any customer environment was successfully exploited through the Able2Shell flaws, though researchers counted 21 compromised servers running the new 4EverAble2Shell chain earlier in the day and scanning activity using the public proof-of-concept code is ongoing.
The company's hosted servers were upgraded to Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26) by November 11, and a follow-up hotfix is in preparation for the two new exploit chains published November 11. N-able says the new server attack needs the Legacy API turned on and exposed to the internet — off by default and not recommended.
Shadowserver counts 148 exposed N-central servers online now, down sharply from 1,338 on Monday. If your provider runs N-central, ask whether the hotfix is applied, whether the Legacy API is off, and what their log review found.
(BleepingComputer · Field Effect · Dark Reading)
Source: bleepingcomputer.com.

item.title: aws/aws-emulator
item.description:
is the fastest-growing repo of the settled November 12 window, gaining over 2,000 stars in a day.
It's Amazon's local emulator of the AWS APIs: point the AWS CLI or an SDK at it and test code against emulated AWS resources with no AWS account. GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance sits second — the Chrome team's curated guides for coding agents, so agents stop writing outdated web code. we-promise/sure (+974/day) is a community-run personal finance app you host yourself, and Alishahryar1/free-claude-code gained 1,381 stars in a day — a way to use Claude Code, Codex and other harnesses for free.
REA kept climbing at +1,631/day. (ghtrends.dev · RepoRadar — November 12 · GitDiscover)
Source: ghtrends.dev.

item.title: Trilateral talks are back on — but Europe's seat at the table is still contested
item.description:
Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner went from the Kremlin to Dublin in a single day, and came out saying the US–Russia–Ukraine talks are running again. "We've restarted it. We've set a new meeting," Witkoff told CNN at Moscow's Vnukovo Airport before flying out. No date or venue was given, and the one concrete result from the whole round remains the prisoner swap agreed in Abu Dhabi — which Zelenskyy called "a real result" in Dublin on Thursday night, saying it will be the biggest exchange of the war. But the two sides are already pulling in different directions over who gets a seat next time.
The day started in Moscow, where the envoys briefed Vladimir Putin for about two hours on the two days of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi — the first direct Russian–Ukrainian discussions in nine months. According to the US official account, the conversation "focused on potential pathways to ending the war, addressing the security concerns of both sides, and establishing the conditions for a durable peace." Witkoff said Putin was invited to give Russia's view of a stable postwar security environment, and Kushner said the US is working on "really incredible" post-war security plans for Ukraine. Putin, for his part, said Russia had "never objected (to) pursuing dialogue" with Europe and wanted a peace that would be "durable and lasting… eternal, for good." Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov called the talks constructive and said Putin will keep discussing Ukraine with Donald Trump at the APEC summit in Shenzhen later this month. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, meanwhile, said the EU is preparing a 22nd sanctions package against Russia, to be presented before the European Council meets on November 26–27.
What each side is saying splits on Europe. The US and Ukraine want Europeans in the room: Witkoff said "they're our partners, and it's important for them to be involved," and Kushner said after the Dublin meeting that "we cannot conclude this deal without the Europeans being at the table." Zelenskyy, speaking at the European Political Community summit in Dublin, said the past days' talks "give (us) hope that we will end this war, that after this meeting will be another meeting and each meeting has to give a result." Moscow is pushing back: Ushakov played down European participation, saying "they are making every effort to get involved in the negotiations, but, as our president has said, they need to decide whether they want peace or a continuation of the war. So far, all their practical actions point precisely to the latter." Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov had already criticised the European presence in Abu Dhabi as not a "promising approach," and the Kremlin said no contacts with EU representatives took place there. And the central issue hasn't moved at all: Kyiv still refuses to surrender the Donbas, and Moscow still demands it.
For ordinary Ukrainians the diplomacy changed nothing on the ground. Russia launched another ballistic missile and drone attack overnight into Thursday — the same barrage covered in the morning brief, which killed a woman in a Kyiv apartment block — and Zelenskyy warned on Thursday that Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink his forces rely on, has faced "significant disruptions" again in recent days. "These are not random errors but systematic speed restrictions," he said. "For us, this primarily means a significant complication in intercepting Russian jet-powered drones." He added on X that the restrictions are "helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes." SpaceX told CNN there had been no change in its service, and the White House and Pentagon did not immediately respond. The same dispute flared in October, when Trump denied approving speed limits on Ukrainian terminals while Musk said the Trump administration was behind them. Kyiv says it is "trying to establish all the circumstances with the American side."
In short: the envoys left Moscow claiming the trilateral process is restarted with a new meeting set and Europeans joining next time — but Moscow's own aides are already downplaying Europe's role, the Donbas deadlock is untouched, and the only agreed outcome so far is the prisoner swap. Watch whether the swap actually happens, and whether a date for the next round appears.
Sources:
Source: cnn.com.

item.title: Houthis claim strikes on Saudi Arabia's oil lifeline as Iran's tanker toll keeps growing
item.description:
Yemen's Houthis said on Thursday they had attacked a pumping station on Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline and an oil facility at Yanbu on the Red Sea coast — the pipeline that now carries about 4 million barrels a day of Saudi crude, roughly 4% of global supply, around the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and the Houthis did not say which day the attacks were carried out. It is the latest turn in a campaign that has already hit the kingdom's airports, an Aramco headquarters tower and its Riyadh financial-district offices, and it comes as Iran's Revolutionary Guards keep raising their claimed toll on shipping: four tankers now, they say, caught fire after hitting mines, two still burning, two more intercepted — plus three more tankers damaged on Thursday.
The details, as far as they can be verified, are thin on the tanker side and sharper on the Saudi side. Reuters reports the Houthi claim on the pipeline and Yanbu facility, and notes the pipeline is what has spared Saudi Arabia — the world's biggest oil exporter — from the worst of the Hormuz shutdown that has crippled its neighbours' exports. The coalition said its air defences destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launched toward the Medina region on Thursday, and Saudi civil defence issued a warning for the Yanbu governorate, the Red Sea terminal complex that handles the kingdom's oil exports and is its main Hormuz bypass. The Houthis again denied targeting Mecca, after Saudi civil defence said two ballistic missiles intercepted on Wednesday had debris fall in the Mecca region, including Sabuhah village. On the shipping side, Iran's account has grown from two supertankers on Wednesday night to four tankers caught fire after mine strikes, with two still burning — but no vessel names, flags, owners or crew conditions have been given, and the maritime reporting body UKMTO has logged only one strike, off Oman on Tuesday. Reuters said it could not independently verify the Iranian reports. The gap between the two counts is now the story: Iran claims a wave of strikes, while the international incident record lists far fewer.
What each side is saying is now a straight contradiction. The Houthis present the pipeline and Yanbu attacks as part of a widening campaign against Saudi airports, ports and oil installations, and have demanded a large financial settlement to stop. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed damage to the pipeline or Yanbu, and its public line remains the intercepts: missiles destroyed, no casualties. Iran's Guards warn the same fate awaits any vessel that turns off its navigation systems and cooperates with the US military on the southern route. Tehran, for its part, is reviewing a US proposal through mediator Pakistan, according to its foreign ministry — while its forces keep the pressure on shipping, with Reuters reporting Iran also attacked ship-navigation systems on Oman's Didamar island in the strait.
For ordinary people the stakes run through fuel prices and flights. The East-West pipeline is Saudi Arabia's workaround for a closed Hormuz; if it were knocked out for long, Reuters reported earlier that stocks at Yanbu could sustain exports for only around five to seven days, and oil has already been volatile on every new incident. The Houthi campaign has also kept Riyadh's King Khalid airport disrupted for days, and the US Embassy still requires special approval for government staff to use Saudi airports. The shipping picture is murkier: Reuters, citing Washington Institute data, counts at least 10 ships hit in the first 10 days of November after 37 attacks in October, and the International Maritime Organization has recorded 133 confirmed incidents in the strait and wider region since February, with 25 seafarers killed.
In short: the Houthis claim they hit the pipeline that lets Saudi oil bypass Hormuz — unconfirmed by Riyadh — while Iran's claimed tanker toll keeps climbing with no independent verification. The verified facts are the Medina intercept, the Yanbu warning, and a pipeline carrying a twentieth of the world's oil now sitting in the crosshairs. Watch for a Saudi damage statement and any UKMTO confirmation of the tanker claims.
Sources:
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Nvidia shares fell as much as 14% after the resignation, then recovered — Bernstein cut its price target in half
item.description:
Nvidia shares opened more than 13% lower on Thursday after Jensen Huang's resignation, dropping as low as $148.80 — a new 52-week low — before recovering to close down 4.34% at $166.19.

Earnings stay on Tuesday, November 17. (CoinDesk · Motley Fool · FinanceFeeds)

item.title: New N-able zero-day "4EverAble2Shell" exploited within hours — 21 servers hit, most on the latest patch
item.description:
Hackers are actively exploiting a newly disclosed N-able N-central zero-day, dubbed 4EverAble2Shell, to compromise servers and deploy cryptocurrency miners — researchers counted at least 21 affected systems, including 19 running the company's latest security update.
Security researcher Sean Bales published proof-of-concept exploits for two new flaws on Thursday morning (4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell), tested against the November 10 hotfix that was supposed to fix the first batch of 30+ zero-days he disclosed earlier in the week. Probing started around 08:30 UTC, hours after publication; by 12:50 UTC researchers counted 21 live Monero miners across seven countries (US, Canada, UK, Germany, France, Sweden, South Africa).
The chain combines an Apache Axis flaw (CVE-2026-90436) with an N-central privilege escalation to get root; it requires the Legacy API to be enabled, which N-able says is off by default and not recommended. N-able's own advisory said it had seen no signs of compromise via the new flaws — the researchers' timestamps say otherwise.
N-central is the management plane MSPs use to run their customers' devices, which is why this one matters beyond the miners: so far the payloads are cryptojacking, but the same access could do far worse. (BleepingComputer · 0daynews)
Source: bleepingcomputer.com.

item.title: Qubole breach: attackers abused a trusted AWS role to raid customer accounts
item.description:
Attackers breached AWS accounts belonging to multiple Qubole customers between October 14 and 26, stealing stored secrets and data by exploiting credentials for an AWS account Qubole's platform uses to access those customer environments.
Cloud security firm Wiz disclosed the incident. Qubole is a cloud data platform that manages compute and storage in customers' AWS accounts through cross-account IAM roles — so the attack abused a trusted third-party relationship rather than breaking into each customer directly.
The number of affected organisations was not disclosed. If you use a platform with cross-account AWS access, this is the one to check your trust roles for.
(defend.network briefing, citing The Hacker News)
Source: defend.network.

item.title: Fridge-hack follow-up: Iran formally rejects France's attribution; two Russian-aligned groups claimed it instead
item.description:
Iran's Foreign Ministry has formally rejected France's attribution of the October supermarket refrigeration attacks to the IRGC's Shahid Kaveh unit, calling the allegations "baseless and hostile."
France named the unit on November 9, citing Farsi-language indicators and IP addresses linked to Iranian infrastructure, and said it would seek EU sanctions. Meanwhile two Russian-aligned hacktivist groups claimed responsibility for the attacks on Wednesday, though their claims have attracted limited credibility.
France's attribution covers only the French attacks on October 11–12 (~700 stores); the second wave of refrigeration incidents reported across Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland earlier this month remains under separate investigation. (ACR Journal · EU Today)
Source: acrjournal.uk.

item.title: cloudflare/security-audit-skill
item.description:
is the biggest weekly gainer on all of GitHub, adding 11,507 stars for a total of ~70,500.
It's a six-phase audit workflow written as markdown for any coding agent that can spawn parallel sub-agents — the agent checks its own findings instead of just flagging them. openai/codex-security (~11,900 stars) is the packaged version of the same idea: a cs CLI, TypeScript SDK, Codex plugin and GitHub Action that scan, validate, patch and verify fixes. Also new: anefzaoui/misterdownloadmanager, a free open-source download manager with the familiar IDM-style window, and NVIDIA/auto-ontology, the week's #1 new repo by stars (+7,947), a library that builds a context layer from enterprise metadata so agents know what data means and where it came from.
(Medium — weekly AI repos · Medium — Day 273 trending · Daily Diff)
Source: medium.com.

item.title: Murdaugh retrial — tomorrow's hearing could throw out all four murder indictments
item.description:
Alex Murdaugh is due back in court Friday, November 13, in Lexington County, where Judge Debra McCaslin will hear the defence's motion to dismiss all four murder indictments. The defence argues SLED's lead agent told the grand jury in July 2022 that an expert had found Maggie and Paul Murdaugh's blood on the shirt Alex wore the night of the killings — eight months after SLED's own lab reported finding no human blood on it. Prosecutors call the agent's year-long miss inadvertent and oppose dismissal. McCaslin has already warned both sides the retrial starts April 5, 2027, "whether you like it or not." (Substack — DeWitt · Parade · True Crime Today)
No fresh developments today in the Netanyahu trial (Attorney General appearance set for Wednesday, November 18) or the FTC v. Amazon cases.
Source: michaeldewittsouthernwriter.substack.com.

item.title: Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia — resigned as CEO after 33 years
item.description:
Jensen Huang has resigned as president, chief executive and a director of Nvidia, effective immediately, the company announced on Thursday morning. The board accepted his resignation on Wednesday, according to a regulatory filing, ending a five-day crisis that began when Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman US officials believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence. Chief financial officer Colette Kress takes over as interim CEO while keeping her finance job, and Harvey Jones, a former Synopsys chief executive who has sat on Nvidia's board since 1993, becomes the company's first-ever board chair.
The resignation came hours after Nvidia's board met late on Wednesday night to decide Huang's future. Reuters reported the meeting citing a source familiar with the matter, and CBS News, citing two sources, reported the board was preparing to remove him. The Wall Street Journal first reported on Wednesday that the board was preparing to oust him, hours after The New York Times reported a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reports to Huang. The first affair, with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed whom US officials believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence, was admitted by Huang in a staff memo on Sunday. Bloomberg reported the board has been working with an outside firm to identify potential replacements.
The company's announcement gave no reason for the departure, instead thanking Huang for his contributions over 33 years. "Jensen's contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry," the company said. The board said operations, customer commitments and the product roadmap will continue without interruption, and the fiscal third-quarter earnings report stays on Tuesday, November 17.
What each side is saying has split along market-versus-company lines. Investors have made up their minds: Nvidia shares were down nearly 12% in early trading on Thursday, and have fallen more than 19% since Friday, wiping out more than $855 billion in market value, according to TechCrunch. CNBC recorded a 10.4% premarket drop. "The market is starting to price Nvidia without its founder as the likely outcome, not a tail risk," portfolio manager Armina Rosenberg of Minotaur Capital told Reuters on Wednesday. "Losing Jensen would be a real blow." Prediction market Polymarket had moved to an 88% chance Huang resigns or is removed by the end of the year, with odds for a successor favouring Ian Buck, who runs the data-centre business. The fallout spread to the companies Nvidia bankrolls: CoreWeave fell about 9% on Thursday, Nebius 16% and IREN 6.6%, while rivals AMD and Broadcom rose after hours on Wednesday.
The deeper worry is succession, not just scandal. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and was its only CEO, running a famously flat organisation with around 60 direct reports and no heir apparent or succession plan — though two of his children work in executive roles. He owns about 3.5% of the company and, unlike most Silicon Valley founders, holds no supervoting rights, so the board could vote him out at any time. TechCrunch notes the stakes go beyond one man: as of the end of the second quarter Nvidia reported $99 billion in investments plus $25 billion in commitments, $36 billion in cloud service commitments, and up to $105 billion in credit guarantees for an OpenAI data centre campus in Ohio — a web of financing for the AI buildout that now has no clear steward. Congress is still in the picture too: the House chairs' request for Huang to appear at a closed-door briefing on November 18 is now in limbo, and Axios reported Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick stalled President Trump's crackdown on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China.
For ordinary people the impact is still mostly market, not product: no interruption to GeForce drivers, product shipments or developer programs has been announced, and demand for Nvidia's chips is not expected to drop in the near term. But analysts warned the wider universe of companies Nvidia finances — largely customers building data centres that will use its chips — could suffer if the turmoil drags on. "In these types of booms or bubbles, sometimes all it takes is a slowdown to shift it into the bust phase," Nick Ferres of Vantage Point Asset Management told Reuters. The next hard dates are earnings on Tuesday, November 17 and the requested Capitol Hill briefing on November 18.
In short: Huang resigned Thursday after the board met Wednesday night; Kress is interim CEO and Jones is the first board chair. The company gave no reason, but the market read it as an ouster — shares down nearly 12% in early trading and more than $855 billion in value gone since Friday.
Sources:
Source: techcrunch.com.

The board accepted his resignation on Wednesday, according to a regulatory filing, ending a five-day crisis that began when Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman US officials believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence. Chief financial officer Colette Kress takes over as interim CEO while keeping her finance job, and Harvey Jones, a former Synopsys chief executive who has sat on Nvidia's board since 1993, becomes the company's first-ever board chair.

The resignation came hours after Nvidia's board met late on Wednesday night to decide Huang's future. Reuters reported the meeting citing a source familiar with the matter, and CBS News, citing two sources, reported the board was preparing to remove him. The Wall Street Journal first reported on Wednesday that the board was preparing to oust him, hours after The New York Times reported a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reports to Huang. The first affair, with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed whom US officials believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence, was admitted by Huang in a staff memo on Sunday. Bloomberg reported the board has been working with an outside firm to identify potential replacements.

The company's announcement gave no reason for the departure, instead thanking Huang for his contributions over 33 years. "Jensen's contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry," the company said. The board said operations, customer commitments and the product roadmap will continue without interruption, and the fiscal third-quarter earnings report stays on Tuesday, November 17.

What each side is saying has split along market-versus-company lines. Investors have made up their minds: Nvidia shares were down nearly 12% in early trading on Thursday, and have fallen more than 19% since Friday, wiping out more than $855 billion in market value, according to TechCrunch. CNBC recorded a 10.4% premarket drop. "The market is starting to price Nvidia without its founder as the likely outcome, not a tail risk," portfolio manager Armina Rosenberg of Minotaur Capital told Reuters on Wednesday. "Losing Jensen would be a real blow." Prediction market Polymarket had moved to an 88% chance Huang resigns or is removed by the end of the year, with odds for a successor favouring Ian Buck, who runs the data-centre business. The fallout spread to the companies Nvidia bankrolls: CoreWeave fell about 9% on Thursday, Nebius 16% and IREN 6.6%, while rivals AMD and Broadcom rose after hours on Wednesday.

The deeper worry is succession, not just scandal. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and was its only CEO, running a famously flat organisation with around 60 direct reports and no heir apparent or succession plan — though two of his children work in executive roles. He owns about 3.5% of the company and, unlike most Silicon Valley founders, holds no supervoting rights, so the board could vote him out at any time. TechCrunch notes the stakes go beyond one man: as of the end of the second quarter Nvidia reported $99 billion in investments plus $25 billion in commitments, $36 billion in cloud service commitments, and up to $105 billion in credit guarantees for an OpenAI data centre campus in Ohio — a web of financing for the AI buildout that now has no clear steward. Congress is still in the picture too: the House chairs' request for Huang to appear at a closed-door briefing on November 18 is now in limbo, and Axios reported Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick stalled President Trump's crackdown on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China.

For ordinary people the impact is still mostly market, not product: no interruption to GeForce drivers, product shipments or developer programs has been announced, and demand for Nvidia's chips is not expected to drop in the near term. But analysts warned the wider universe of companies Nvidia finances — largely customers building data centres that will use its chips — could suffer if the turmoil drags on. "In these types of booms or bubbles, sometimes all it takes is a slowdown to shift it into the bust phase," Nick Ferres of Vantage Point Asset Management told Reuters. The next hard dates are earnings on Tuesday, November 17 and the requested Capitol Hill briefing on November 18.

In short: Huang resigned Thursday after the board met Wednesday night; Kress is interim CEO and Jones is the first board chair. The company gave no reason, but the market read it as an ouster — shares down nearly 12% in early trading and more than $855 billion in value gone since Friday.

item.title: Russia hit Kyiv overnight as US envoys met Putin in Moscow — no outcome announced yet
item.description:
Russia launched a large combined overnight attack on Ukraine starting at 18:00 on Wednesday, striking Kyiv and multiple regions with ballistic missiles, anti-ship missiles and 123 strike drones, hours before US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff sat down with Vladimir Putin in Moscow. In Kyiv's Solomyanskyi district a Russian drone hit a nine-storey residential building, setting floors three through six ablaze and killing a 44-year-old woman; five people were injured, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Ukrainian air defences reported 94 targets neutralised by 08:00, with damage recorded across eight regions. Russia said it downed five Ukrainian drones heading for Moscow and 71 across Russia overnight.
The details show a deliberate escalation on the night the diplomacy resumed. Russia's Defence Ministry said it had hit a rocket factory in Kyiv and a drone assembly workshop and missile fuel factory in the wider Kyiv region, as well as electricity substations in the western Zhytomyr region, and local officials reported damage to energy and civilian infrastructure in the north-western Rivne region. Ukrainian reporting, via h.ua, says the attack used Iskander-M, KN-23 and S-400 ballistic missiles, Tsirkon anti-ship missiles and 123 strike drones, including 73 jet-powered Shaheds. Moscow's claims about which military facilities were destroyed could not be independently verified. The timing matters: the strikes landed the same night the Abu Dhabi talks ended with only a prisoner-swap agreement, and hours before the envoys' Moscow meeting.
In Moscow, Kushner and Witkoff arrived on Thursday for what Reuters called the latest push for a peace deal, the 10th time Witkoff has met Putin in person. According to RIA Novosti, Witkoff told Putin that Donald Trump was seeking to end the war as quickly as possible, and described the Abu Dhabi discussions as having taken place in a constructive spirit. Kushner discussed preliminary conversations with European countries about the continent's postwar security arrangements, and Witkoff said he hoped to announce "shortly, hopefully maybe even at the end of this meeting, the next trilateral meeting that will include the Europeans." Putin responded that Moscow had never objected to dialogue with European governments, and said he wanted a peace that would be "durable and lasting… eternal, for good." Putin also proposed a humanitarian initiative involving Kostyantynivka, a frontline city in eastern Ukraine. Axios reports the US is pushing a new Europe-Russia security framework as part of the peace push, with the envoys expected to ask Russia to submit a proposal for a security agreement with Europe and to allow European representatives into the next round of talks.
What each side is saying has not moved. Kyiv has strongly rejected Putin's demands to surrender the whole of the eastern Donbas region in return for peace, and with talks deadlocked on land, the prisoner swap — 1,000-for-1,000, possibly 1,500, the biggest of the war — remains the only concrete outcome of the Abu Dhabi round, with numbers to be finalised in Moscow. Medinsky, Russia's chief negotiator, said the sides had "moved closer to peace" but that Moscow's baseline demands were unchanged. No outcome statement from the Moscow meeting had been published by the time of this brief; the envoys are due in Dublin on Thursday night to meet Zelenskyy, who is attending the sidelines of an EU leaders' summit there.
For ordinary people in Ukraine the night meant more of the same grinding toll: another residential building hit, another death in the capital, and more energy infrastructure damaged as winter approaches, with power outages already running into the hundreds of thousands in the east after the grid campaign of the past two weeks. For everyone else the stakes run through energy and shipping: the war's escalation and the Hormuz campaign together have kept oil volatile, with Brent around $92–93 this week.
In short: Russia hit Kyiv with missiles and drones overnight, killing one woman in an apartment block, on the same day US envoys met Putin to push a Europe-Russia security framework and a next trilateral round including Europeans — but no outcome from the Moscow meeting had been announced yet, and the envoys head to Dublin tonight to brief Zelenskyy.
Sources:
Source: kwsn.com.

item.title: Hormuz — IRGC claims two supertankers exploded Wednesday night; no names, unverified
item.description:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said on Thursday that two supertankers carrying more than 4 million barrels of oil combined were disabled by massive explosions in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday night after ignoring warnings against using an "unauthorised" southern shipping route.
Iranian state media later said the tankers had exploded after hitting naval mines, though the Guards' own statement did not specify the cause. No vessel names, flags, owners or crew conditions have been given, and UKMTO has issued no matching confirmation.
The Guards warned the same fate awaits any vessel that turns off its navigation systems and cooperates with the US military on the southern route. Treat the claim as unverified — it rests entirely on an Iranian military statement.
(Reuters via MarineLink · PressTV · Vocemundi)
Source: marinelink.com.

item.title: Houthi/Saudi — debris from intercepted missiles fell in the Mecca region
item.description:
Saudi Arabia said debris from two ballistic missiles intercepted by its air defences fell in the Mecca region on Wednesday, as the kingdom and the Houthis continued trading attacks.
Saudi state television identified the locations as Sabuhah village, about 35 km northeast of the Grand Mosque in Mecca, and Wadi al-Maghmas, about 21 km east of the mosque. The Houthis have repeatedly denied Saudi accusations that they target Mecca and Medina, saying their military operations are directed at military and strategic targets elsewhere in Saudi Arabia.
This is follow-up detail to Wednesday's intercepts already covered in the evening brief (three cruise missiles toward Riyadh, two drones toward Mecca and the south, two missiles west — all intercepted, no casualties). No new Houthi attacks were reported overnight.
(Reuters via FroggyWeb)
Source: froggyweb.com.

item.title: Apple HomeView reviews land today; hub ships tomorrow, accessories orderable Friday
item.description:
Reviews of Apple's $299 HomeView smart-home hub published this morning ahead of its Friday, November 13 launch, and Apple said select Apple Home Collection accessories will be available to order starting Friday, with availability beginning in December — some accessories not until early 2027.
MacRumors also reports Apple plans a December software update for HomeView with a fix for a Siri issue found in review. HomeView (7" display, A18, Siri AI beta, tabletop + wall-mount) and the 4th-gen Apple TV 4K ($299, A19) ship November 13; HomePod mini 2 ($149) shipped October 30.
(MacRumors)
Source: macrumors.com.

item.title: KEV watch — the November 9 four are due today; no new additions
item.description:
No new CISA KEV additions were published overnight.
The federal patch deadline for the four flaws added November 9 falls today, November 12: SSHole (CVE-2026-123158, OpenSSH), GPUStack auth bypass (CVE-2026-102895, CVSS 9.8 — GPUStack's advisory says it was exploited against a 2.1.1 deployment, where attackers created backends running reverse shells), FreeSWITCH code injection (CVE-2026-116779) and IBM Aspera Faspex (CVE-2026-123218). The Barracuda pair is due tomorrow, November 13; the six added November 10 (including the Chrome zero-day CVE-2026-125350 and Outlook CVE-2026-124194) are due November 24.
The KEV catalog now lists 1,779 entries. (Pandromeda · ImmunitySec KEV)
Source: pandromeda.com.

item.title: GitHub trending, November 12 — agent guardrails lead the day
item.description:
meta/astryx is still the fastest-growing repo (+2.8k/day, ~24.6k stars).
New names surfacing today: GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src — browser-vendor curated guides (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, MDN teams) to keep coding agents on the modern web; shadcn/improve — an agent skill that audits a codebase and writes implementation plans for cheaper models to carry out (~11.2k stars, +361/day); aws/aws-emulator — test code against AWS APIs locally with no AWS account; pingdotgg/t3code — one control surface for every coding agent on your machine, from the T3 team; NotRexed/Hookshot — a native recompilation of the Zelda: Ocarina of Time Switch 2 remake (+1,190/day, ~8.3k). Still leading overall: REA (~451k), storytold/craft-anything (~29.3k, +1,615/day), janestreet/agent_skills (~7k, +2,205/day), Lee-xeo/Claude-Cage (+2,217/day), huamidev/GestaltX.
(GitDiscover · GhTrends Nov 12 · Trendar · Daily Diff)
Source: gitdiscover.org.

item.title: Netanyahu trial — judges order the Attorney General to appear next Wednesday
item.description:
The panel hearing Benjamin Netanyahu's corruption trial ordered Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara on Thursday to appear at the Jerusalem District Court on Wednesday, November 18, at 9:30 a.m. to discuss how the proceedings are being managed and the options for moving them forward.
The decision follows her refusal to attend a proposed discussion, conveyed to the court by prosecutors a day earlier. This follows the defence's request to summon her after former Attorney General Avichai Mandelblit's testimony about the authorisation of investigative actions in Cases 1000, 2000 and 4000; prosecutor Yehudit Tirosh has pushed back against the summons while signalling openness to a negotiated resolution.
(JBizNews · Haaretz notification)
Source: jbiznews.com.

item.title: FTC v. Amazon — unredacted ads complaint: prices raised up to 50%, 250% on Prime Day
item.description:
The FTC and 22 states filed an updated, unredacted version of their complaint against Amazon over its online search advertising auction, alleging Amazon secretly raises advertising prices by as much as 50% above auction results on ordinary days and by as much as 250% on major shopping days like Prime Day or Black Friday, misleading advertisers about the true cause. The suit was filed in August in the Western District of Washington. Separately, the economics hearing in the FTC's antitrust case continued, with Judge Chun pressing the FTC on consumer harm; the FTC conceded it cannot quantify a but-for world. The Prime "dark patterns" jury trial continues in Seattle. (FTC · Typefully — economics hearing)
No fresh developments in the Murdaugh retrial (next hearing Friday, November 13).
Source: ftc.gov.

item.title: Nvidia's board met late Wednesday to decide Jensen Huang's future — still no decision announced
item.description:
Nvidia's board met late on Wednesday night to decide whether to oust founder and chief executive Jensen Huang, Reuters reported, citing a source familiar with the matter. CBS News, citing two sources, also reported the board is preparing to remove him soon. As of late Wednesday night there was still no decision announced, no interim chief named, and no company statement — Huang remains CEO. Bloomberg reported the board has been working with an outside firm to identify potential replacements, and is weighing whether to name an interim chief while it searches.
The meeting marks a sharp turn from Sunday, when the board said it had confidence in Huang and his leadership team. Under Nvidia's bylaws Huang can be removed "with or without cause" by a majority vote of the directors — there are 11, and all but Huang are independent. The Wall Street Journal first reported on Wednesday that the board was preparing to oust him, hours after The New York Times reported a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reports to Huang. The first affair, with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed whom US officials believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence, was admitted by Huang in a staff memo on Sunday.
What each side is saying has not changed much, but the market has made up its mind about the direction of travel. Nvidia's shares fell 8.6% in after-hours trading to $158.84, and Reuters reports that if those losses hold, the company will have lost about $600 billion in market value since the board announced its investigation. "The market is starting to price Nvidia without its founder as the likely outcome, not a tail risk," portfolio manager Armina Rosenberg of Minotaur Capital told Reuters. "Losing Jensen would be a real blow." Prediction market Polymarket moved to an 88% chance Huang resigns or is removed by the end of the year, with odds for a successor favouring Ian Buck, who runs the data-centre business. Rosenberg said chief financial officer Colette Kress, in the role for more than a decade, would be the natural interim choice — but the harder question is who leads the technology roadmap longer term, since Huang, 63, has no obvious successor, owns about 3.6% of the company, and has dozens of direct reports. The fallout spread wider: Nasdaq futures sank 1%, Micron fell nearly 2% and CoreWeave dropped 6% after hours, while rivals AMD and Broadcom rose 4% and 3%.
One new strand landed on Wednesday: Axios reported, citing high-level sources, that US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick stalled President Trump's crackdown on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China. The White House and a spokesperson for Lutnick did not immediately respond. Trump has said he has not discussed the allegations with Huang but has voiced support for him. The congressional clock is still running too — the House chairs' 5 p.m. ET deadline to agree to a closed-door briefing on November 18 passed with a subpoena threat on the table, as covered in this evening's brief.
For ordinary people the impact is still mostly market, not product: no interruption to GeForce drivers, product shipments or developer programs has been announced, and demand for Nvidia's chips is not expected to drop in the near term. But analysts warned the wider universe of companies Nvidia finances — largely customers building data centres that will use its chips — could suffer if the turmoil drags on. "In these types of booms or bubbles, sometimes all it takes is a slowdown to shift it into the bust phase," Nick Ferres of Vantage Point Asset Management told Reuters. The next hard dates are earnings on November 17 and the requested Capitol Hill briefing on November 18.
In short: the board met late Wednesday to decide Huang's future, with CBS confirming the ouster preparation and Bloomberg reporting a successor search is under way — but nothing has been announced yet, and Huang is still CEO. The market is now pricing in his departure.
Sources:
Source: kwsn.com.

"Losing Jensen would be a real blow." Prediction market Polymarket moved to an 88% chance Huang resigns or is removed by the end of the year, with odds for a successor favouring Ian Buck, who runs the data-centre business. Rosenberg said chief financial officer Colette Kress, in the role for more than a decade, would be the natural interim choice — but the harder question is who leads the technology roadmap longer term, since Huang, 63, has no obvious successor, owns about 3.6% of the company, and has dozens of direct reports. The fallout spread wider: Nasdaq futures sank 1%, Micron fell nearly 2% and CoreWeave dropped 6% after hours, while rivals AMD and Broadcom rose 4% and 3%.

One new strand landed on Wednesday: Axios reported, citing high-level sources, that US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick stalled President Trump's crackdown on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China. The White House and a spokesperson for Lutnick did not immediately respond. Trump has said he has not discussed the allegations with Huang but has voiced support for him. The congressional clock is still running too — the House chairs' 5 p.m. ET deadline to agree to a closed-door briefing on November 18 passed with a subpoena threat on the table, as covered in this evening's brief.

For ordinary people the impact is still mostly market, not product: no interruption to GeForce drivers, product shipments or developer programs has been announced, and demand for Nvidia's chips is not expected to drop in the near term. But analysts warned the wider universe of companies Nvidia finances — largely customers building data centres that will use its chips — could suffer if the turmoil drags on. "In these types of booms or bubbles, sometimes all it takes is a slowdown to shift it into the bust phase," Nick Ferres of Vantage Point Asset Management told Reuters. The next hard dates are earnings on November 17 and the requested Capitol Hill briefing on November 18.

In short: the board met late Wednesday to decide Huang's future, with CBS confirming the ouster preparation and Bloomberg reporting a successor search is under way — but nothing has been announced yet, and Huang is still CEO. The market is now pricing in his departure.

item.title: Iran struck navigation systems on Oman's Didamar Island — the first attack on Omani soil in the Hormuz campaign
item.description:
Iran has attacked ship navigation systems on Didamar, a small Omani island also known as Little Quoin that sits beside the southern traffic corridor of the Strait of Hormuz, three sources with knowledge of the matter confirmed to Reuters on Wednesday. Iranian state media said on Tuesday that the Revolutionary Guards' navy carried out strikes destroying "enemy navigation systems" on the island. The Institute for the Study of War identified the attack as having happened on November 8, before Iranian state media claimed responsibility on November 10.
The attack itself is confirmed; the damage is not. The three sources gave Reuters no damage assessment, and Reuters said it could not determine independently whether any navigation systems were destroyed. Reuters did verify video showing smoke rising from the island, and imagery from the EU's Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellite showed scorch marks and thermal activity near the radar and radio equipment. The Institute for the Study of War likewise questioned the extent of the reported damage, noting that commercial vessels kept using the southern route after the attack.
What each side says: Iranian state television said the personnel and equipment on the island were "helping the flow of oil smuggling by the enemy" — meaning the tankers that have kept using the southern route with American support. A Guards navy official added that no vessel Iran considers unauthorised had passed through the route overnight, and a separate Iranian statement blamed the destruction of what it called US coastal radar and navigation aids for raising the risk to ships using illegal passages. Shipping and maritime-security sources told Reuters the strike would likely have only limited impact on commercial traffic, because other navigation systems are in place elsewhere. Neither US Central Command nor Oman's media ministry immediately responded to requests for comment.
The human impact runs through oil and shipping costs rather than the island itself — Didamar is uninhabited rock with a lighthouse dating to 1914 and shore radar and radio gear used to track vessels and coordinate traffic at the entrance to the Gulf. The island belongs to Oman, which makes the strike politically sensitive: Oman's foreign minister discussed joint mechanisms for the strait with Iran's foreign minister as recently as November 5, and Oman has been a mediator in the conflict. The attack followed US strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island on November 2. It also comes as Gulf oil exports have recovered to more than 80% of pre-war levels in September and October, helped by US military-assisted flows through the strait and higher Saudi exports via the Red Sea port of Yanbu — the recovery Iran's campaign is trying to break.
In short: Iran hit navigation gear on an Omani island in the strait on November 8, the first strike on Omani soil in this campaign. The attack is confirmed by three sources to Reuters, but whether the systems were actually destroyed is still unclear, and shipping sources expect limited disruption.
Sources:
Source: wncy.com.

item.title: Russell Brand jailed for ten and a half years — catch-up from Monday that earlier briefs missed
item.description:
Russell Brand was sentenced on Monday, November 9, at Southwark Crown Court in London to ten years and six months in prison, after a jury convicted him last Thursday of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault against four women, for offences between 2004 and 2009. He was acquitted of two further counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault. He must serve two-thirds of the sentence — around seven years — before he can be released on licence, and will be on the sex offenders' register for life.
The sentence breaks down as nine years for the rape of a 21-year-old fan in 2009, after meeting her at a stand-up show at the Hammersmith Apollo, plus 18 months, nine months and eight months for the three sexual assaults, running concurrently with each other but consecutively to the rape sentence. The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, told Brand he had become "a sexual predator" as he was becoming famous, and that he had displayed "staggering arrogance" and "an arrogant disregard for a woman's right to say no". The judge said Brand's fame had protected him until 2023, when a joint investigation by The Times, The Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches prompted women to come forward. The Metropolitan Police investigation, Operation Actinolite, involved more than 100 witnesses and over 1,400 documents.
Brand, 51, has denied all the charges throughout and maintains he never had sex without consent. His wife Laura Gallacher, with whom he has three children, was in court for the sentencing and, according to his defence barrister Ian Winter KC, has no intention of leaving him; Brand mouthed "I love you" to her as he left the dock, the BBC reported. Outside the courtroom, the verdict has split opinion: commentators Megyn Kelly and Elon Musk have publicly questioned the trial's integrity, calling it a "political witch hunt", while the judge's sentencing remarks stressed the significant and lasting harm suffered by the victims.
The case is not fully closed. The Metropolitan Police have confirmed Brand remains under investigation over two further rape allegations, and detectives are assessing additional reports received since the conviction. Page Six reported on Tuesday that a new accuser in the United States has come forward and is in contact with attorney Gloria Allred — that report is single-source and unconfirmed. Brand is reported to be considering an appeal, though legal observers cited by the Daily Mail suggested the jury's mixed verdicts could make a successful challenge difficult.
In short: Brand was jailed for ten and a half years on Monday for one rape and three sexual assaults, with the judge calling him a "sexual predator" whose fame shielded him — and police are still investigating two further rape allegations against him.
Sources:
Source: thetimes.com.

item.title: Ukraine — capitals traded strikes overnight as US envoys head to Moscow (developing)
item.description:
Russia and Ukraine exchanged attacks on each other's capitals early on Thursday, a day after the Abu Dhabi peace talks ended and as US envoys were set to travel to Moscow to meet President Vladimir Putin.
Explosions were heard in Kyiv in the early hours of Thursday, a Reuters witness said, though it was not immediately clear whether the city had incurred damage. Russia said it downed five drones heading for Moscow, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram, without giving further details.
Developing — only the Reuters wire so far, no casualty or damage figures yet. (Reuters via WIXX)
Source: wixx.com.

item.title: Abu Dhabi follow-up — US pushing a Europe-Russia security framework; Putin meeting Thursday morning
item.description:
Axios reports the US is pushing a new Europe-Russia security framework as part of the peace push: Kushner and Witkoff are expected to reiterate Trump's request that Russia submit a proposal for a security agreement with Europe, including steps to ease tensions, and to urge Putin to allow European representatives into the next round of Russia-Ukraine talks.
Putin aide Yuri Ushakov confirmed the meeting will take place on Thursday morning: "We don't yet know the results of the talks in Abu Dhabi. But they're bringing something."
After Moscow, the envoys are expected to travel to Dublin to meet Zelenskyy on Thursday night. Russian negotiator Vladimir Medinsky said the two sides had "moved closer to peace."
The prisoner-swap agreement from Abu Dhabi — the biggest of the war, numbers to be finalised in Moscow — stands as covered in this evening's brief. (Axios via The Tribune · CNN)
Source: thetribune-sortd-pro.demo.sortd.mobi.
