item.title: Maersk confirms data breach as WhiteArmor ransomware gang demands $5 million
item.description:
Shipping giant Maersk confirmed on Wednesday that an attacker gained unauthorised access to a local legacy system inherited through an earlier acquisition and extracted data.
The company said the incident is isolated, contained, and that it expects no disruption to operations, with no indication of impact on other Maersk systems or on customer and partner systems connected via APIs and EDI. It did not name the system, the type of data taken, or when the intrusion happened.
The WhiteArmor ransomware gang listed Maersk on its leak site over the weekend and is demanding $5 million in bitcoin within 30 days, claiming about 100GB stolen from the OCF/LF Logistics platform — the system of LF Logistics, which Maersk acquired in 2022 — including nearly 30,000 driver records. The gang also claimed plaintext passwords were taken; Maersk told Cybernews that passwords are stored in protected form and that what the attackers stole were single-use codes that have since expired.
Maersk confirmed to Cybernews that its breach is the same incident WhiteArmor claims, but has not confirmed the gang's data claims. (BleepingComputer · Cybernews · Neowin)
Source: bleepingcomputer.com.

item.title: N0n ransomware group claims DraftKings and LiveRamp data exposures (unverified)
item.description:
The N0n ransomware group listed two big names on November 11, both so far only tracker reports with no company confirmation.
DraftKings: a leak marked "NOT PAID — EXPOSED" containing 6.3 million mobile device advertising identifiers from 2020 and 7.4 million hashed consumer email addresses from 2020, plus campaign demographic analytics from November 2019. LiveRamp: 39,055 files totalling 2.2 terabytes, including identity graph feeds and 19.2 million hashed email identities the group says are resolved to named individuals, dated October 2026.
Both are claims from ransomware trackers, not confirmed breaches — the companies have not commented. (QPulse — DraftKings · DeXpose — LiveRamp)
Source: qpulse.quasarcybertech.com.

The federal patch deadline for the four flaws added November 9 — SSHole (CVE-2026-123158), GPUStack (CVE-2026-102895), FreeSWITCH (CVE-2026-116779) and IBM Aspera Faspex (CVE-2026-123218) — falls tomorrow, November 12. item.title: Nvidia's board is preparing to oust Jensen Huang — hours after a second affair was reported
item.description:
Nvidia's board is preparing to remove its founder and chief executive, Jensen Huang, after reports of two extramarital affairs — one with a woman US intelligence officials believe is a Chinese spy, and a second, reported today, with a Nvidia executive who reports to him. The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday, citing people familiar with the matter, that the board is preparing to meet as soon as today to determine Huang's future. No final decision has been announced, and Huang remains CEO. Nvidia's shares fell about 8% in after-hours trading on the news.
The second affair was reported earlier on Wednesday by The New York Times, citing five people who worked at the company. The other party is Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reports to Huang. Two of the sources told the Times the pair were videotaped being affectionate at a San Jose hotel during a Nvidia conference in March — the paper says it has not seen the video — and three people briefed on the incident said Huang's security then cornered the person filming and tried to get them to sign a non-disclosure agreement. The Times contacted Huang by phone; he replied, "I don't think you should be talking to me directly," and hung up. Neither Nvidia nor Powell responded to the Times's request for comment. Such relationships are barred under Nvidia's corporate policy.
The first affair, with Alice Huang — a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer whom US officials believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence — was admitted by Huang in a staff memo on Sunday, November 8, the same day the board opened an independent investigation, now led by former acting US Attorney Joon H. Kim and the firm Wachtell Lipton. The board has said it has "no reason to believe" national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but called that a preliminary position. On Wednesday, Nvidia told CNBC that "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption." The New York Times also reported on Tuesday, via Reuters, that Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefed President Trump aboard Air Force One in May about US intelligence indicating Huang was involved with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.
The pressure is also coming from Congress, and today is the deadline. Three House Republican chairs — Brian Mast (Foreign Affairs), John Moolenaar (China committee) and Rick Crawford (Intelligence) — asked Huang on November 4 to attend a closed-door joint briefing on November 18 and to answer by today. Moolenaar said on Fox Business on Wednesday that Huang had until 5 p.m. ET to agree or offer another date, and that if he does not, "I believe there will likely be subpoenas for him to appear." Mast said his committee was preparing a subpoena, and Reuters reported, citing a person familiar with the discussions, that the lawmakers are unlikely to let Huang send his general counsel in his place. No subpoena has been issued, and Nvidia has not publicly said whether Huang will attend. One complication for the lawmakers: Republicans lose control of House committees in January, so a subpoena issued now would likely lapse and need to be reissued by Democrats. Senator Kevin Cramer, a North Dakota Republican, became the first sitting senator to call on Huang to step down on Tuesday, and Baird downgraded Nvidia to Neutral on Wednesday, slashing its price target to $200 from $500.
What each side argues has barely changed, but the stakes have. Lawmakers say the reported relationship raises a national-security question about who has access to the world's most important AI chips and want answers under oath or in a closed briefing. Nvidia's position is that its own checks found no evidence its chips were diverted, that Megaspeed denies diverting them, and that the board's independent inquiry will examine all available information. The board's move today is about the second affair as much as the first: a subordinate relationship is a straightforward policy violation, and it is what appears to have pushed a usually deferential board toward acting before its own investigation finishes. For ordinary people, the immediate impact is market, not product: Nvidia is down roughly $1.7 trillion in value since October 6, and the company reports earnings on November 17 — the day before the requested Capitol Hill briefing.
In short: the board is preparing to decide Huang's future as soon as tonight, after the Times reported a second affair with a subordinate, while Congress's 5 p.m. deadline for him to agree to a November 18 briefing passes with a subpoena threat on the table. Nothing is final yet — no decision announced, no subpoena issued — but the founder-CEO of the world's most valuable AI chipmaker is now fighting on three fronts at once: his board, Congress, and the market.
Sources:
Source: wsj.com.

Nvidia's board is preparing to remove its founder and chief executive, Jensen Huang, after reports of two extramarital affairs — one with a woman US intelligence officials believe is a Chinese spy, and a second, reported today, with a Nvidia executive who reports to him. The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday, citing people familiar with the matter, that the board is preparing to meet as soon as today to determine Huang's future. No final decision has been announced, and Huang remains CEO. Nvidia's shares fell about 8% in after-hours trading on the news.

The second affair was reported earlier on Wednesday by The New York Times, citing five people who worked at the company. The other party is Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reports to Huang. Two of the sources told the Times the pair were videotaped being affectionate at a San Jose hotel during a Nvidia conference in March — the paper says it has not seen the video — and three people briefed on the incident said Huang's security then cornered the person filming and tried to get them to sign a non-disclosure agreement. The Times contacted Huang by phone; he replied, "I don't think you should be talking to me directly," and hung up. Neither Nvidia nor Powell responded to the Times's request for comment. Such relationships are barred under Nvidia's corporate policy.

The first affair, with Alice Huang — a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer whom US officials believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence — was admitted by Huang in a staff memo on Sunday, November 8, the same day the board opened an independent investigation, now led by former acting US Attorney Joon H. Kim and the firm Wachtell Lipton. The board has said it has "no reason to believe" national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but called that a preliminary position. On Wednesday, Nvidia told CNBC that "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption." The New York Times also reported on Tuesday, via Reuters, that Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefed President Trump aboard Air Force One in May about US intelligence indicating Huang was involved with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.

The pressure is also coming from Congress, and today is the deadline. Three House Republican chairs — Brian Mast (Foreign Affairs), John Moolenaar (China committee) and Rick Crawford (Intelligence) — asked Huang on November 4 to attend a closed-door joint briefing on November 18 and to answer by today. Moolenaar said on Fox Business on Wednesday that Huang had until 5 p.m. ET to agree or offer another date, and that if he does not, "I believe there will likely be subpoenas for him to appear." Mast said his committee was preparing a subpoena, and Reuters reported, citing a person familiar with the discussions, that the lawmakers are unlikely to let Huang send his general counsel in his place. No subpoena has been issued, and Nvidia has not publicly said whether Huang will attend. One complication for the lawmakers: Republicans lose control of House committees in January, so a subpoena issued now would likely lapse and need to be reissued by Democrats. Senator Kevin Cramer, a North Dakota Republican, became the first sitting senator to call on Huang to step down on Tuesday, and Baird downgraded Nvidia to Neutral on Wednesday, slashing its price target to $200 from $500.

What each side argues has barely changed, but the stakes have. Lawmakers say the reported relationship raises a national-security question about who has access to the world's most important AI chips and want answers under oath or in a closed briefing. Nvidia's position is that its own checks found no evidence its chips were diverted, that Megaspeed denies diverting them, and that the board's independent inquiry will examine all available information. The board's move today is about the second affair as much as the first: a subordinate relationship is a straightforward policy violation, and it is what appears to have pushed a usually deferential board toward acting before its own investigation finishes. For ordinary people, the immediate impact is market, not product: Nvidia is down roughly $1.7 trillion in value since October 6, and the company reports earnings on November 17 — the day before the requested Capitol Hill briefing.

In short: the board is preparing to decide Huang's future as soon as tonight, after the Times reported a second affair with a subordinate, while Congress's 5 p.m. deadline for him to agree to a November 18 briefing passes with a subpoena threat on the table. Nothing is final yet — no decision announced, no subpoena issued — but the founder-CEO of the world's most valuable AI chipmaker is now fighting on three fronts at once: his board, Congress, and the market.

item.title: Abu Dhabi follow-up — "biggest" prisoner swap agreed, numbers to be set in Moscow tomorrow
item.description:
The Abu Dhabi talks ended Wednesday with one concrete result beyond what this morning's brief reported: Jared Kushner said the sides agreed to "the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners" of the war, with the exact numbers to be finalised when he and Steve Witkoff meet Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday.
Both delegations confirmed the exchange in principle — Ukraine's Rustem Umerov and Russia's Vladimir Medinsky — though no figure was given; the scale discussed was 1,000-for-1,000, possibly 1,500. The Kremlin confirmed Thursday's meeting, and the envoys will then fly to Dublin to meet Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who is attending the European Political Community summit.
Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that progress "hinges on US approach to Russia" and that Kyiv hoped for concrete results this year. The one open fight is Europe's role: Russia declined to meet European officials in Abu Dhabi and, per EU reporting, rejected an EU role in the talks; Kushner said he will raise broadening the talks to include the Europeans with Putin.
(NY Post · Reuters · EU Perspectives)
Source: nypost.com.

item.title: Ukraine grid — follow-up to last night's strikes: 3 killed in Belgorod, Kyiv on water fountains, Crimea blacked out
item.description:
The overnight strikes covered in this morning's brief kept rippling through Wednesday.
Al Jazeera reports Ukrainian drone strikes killed three people in Russia's Belgorod region — up from the one death reported this morning — while in Ukraine, Russia's attacks on power generation and substations in nine regions left hours-long power and water outages across Kyiv and surrounding areas. Residents in the capital were urged to use public drinking-water fountains, and emergency centres offering hot tea and power points to charge devices were set up in the worst-hit areas.
There were also power outages in Crimea, home to about 2.5 million people, after Ukrainian strikes hit energy infrastructure overnight; Russia's Energy Ministry said temporary outage schedules were in force. Russia's Defence Ministry said it downed 709 Ukrainian drones across 14 regions, Crimea and the Black and Azov seas — a Russian claim, unverified.
(Al Jazeera)
Source: aljazeeranews-3fuh52rgrl.edgeone.app.

item.title: Hormuz — another tanker incident Wednesday, and two named ships hit this week
item.description:
The attacks on shipping have not stopped while the US and Iran argue over whether they are even talking.
Iran's army said on Wednesday that a tanker caught fire after striking a naval mine in the eastern Strait of Hormuz, in what it called a prohibited area — an Iranian claim, not independently confirmed. Britain's UKMTO confirmed only that it received a report of an incident involving a tanker in the strait, without identifying the vessel, the crew's status, the damage or the cause.
Two ships are now named this week: India's shipping minister said the Saudi-flagged tanker NCC FAJR, carrying three Indian seafarers, was involved in a "possible attack" while transiting the strait on Wednesday — all crew safe — and the Liberia-flagged VLCC MT FUJAIRAH ENERGY was hit by a projectile on Tuesday while travelling from Al Ruwais to Dubai, injuring four crew including one Indian national. Reuters reports at least 10 ships hit in the first 10 days of November after 37 in October, the highest monthly total since the war began, and the International Maritime Organization has confirmed 133 incidents in the region since late February, with at least 25 seafarers killed.
Oil rebounded on Wednesday after touching two-month lows, as the fresh attacks weakened hopes that a US-Iran de-escalation would quickly restore normal energy flows. On the diplomacy side, Iran's foreign ministry said Tehran was reviewing a US proposal and would convey its view to mediator Pakistan, while Rubio, speaking in Paris after G7 meetings, said he asked other G7 countries to help protect shipping through the strait — and got no takers.
(BOE Report / Reuters · Daily Jagran (NCC FAJR / FUJAIRAH ENERGY) · Pollar News · HeadlinesXtra (oil rebound))
Source: boereport.com.

item.title: Houthi/Saudi — Wednesday's Riyadh attack confirmed by Reuters: 3 cruise missiles, plus drones aimed at Mecca
item.description:
What this morning's brief had as a single-source developing item is now confirmed by Reuters: Saudi air defences intercepted Houthi missiles and drones launched towards Riyadh, Mecca and other regions on Wednesday.
The coalition said it destroyed three cruise missiles headed for the Riyadh region, two drones aimed at Mecca and southern areas, and two missiles pointed west. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree later denied targeting Mecca, saying the group's operations target oil facilities and military bases.
Saudi civil defence issued alerts warning of potential danger in Taif, Yanbu and Khamis Mushait later on Wednesday, then announced the danger had passed. No casualties or damage were reported.
Wednesday's interceptions were the second consecutive day of Houthi missiles launched towards Riyadh, and the third attack on the capital in four days — an all-cruise-missile salvo, which gives radars far less warning than a ballistic missile fired from Yemen. (Reuters via KTWB · Silent Dossier)
Source: ktwb.com.

item.title: Poland — Nawrocki marched with nationalists on Independence Day; no Tusk meeting happened
item.description:
Polish President Karol Nawrocki joined hundreds of thousands of right-wing demonstrators at the annual Independence Day march in Warsaw on Wednesday — city officials put the crowd at about 250,000, organisers at half a million or more — days after the Krakow shooting that authorities attribute to a far-right gunman.
Nawrocki, a conservative nationalist, walked at the front of a crowd stretching more than 3 km, under the slogan "Poles are masters of their own land." Prime Minister Donald Tusk attended a separate rally in Szczecin and said in a video posted to X: "Today, on November 11th, we were supposed to reach out to one another.
Mr. President, we were meant to meet" — the meeting the two had been expected to hold before Independence Day did not happen. Tusk later wrote that Nawrocki "could have tried to unite Poles rather than divide them."
Warsaw police said 59 people were detained in the capital, mostly for drugs, drone-ban breaches and pyrotechnics. Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek said the Krakow attacker had been interested in Anders Behring Breivik, the Norwegian far-right extremist who killed 77 people in 2011.
(AP via EuropeSays · Reuters via KWSN)
Source: europesays.com.

item.title: Israel — Eisenkot pledges fast legislation before a government is even formed
item.description:
With no coalition yet, Gadi Eisenkot's bloc is moving to use the Knesset it now effectively controls: Le Monde reports the bloc aims to move quickly on legislation, with the first major law creating a commission of inquiry, with investigative powers, into the October 7, 2023 security failure and Netanyahu's personal responsibility.
The coalition also intends to begin rolling back laws passed by the previous Knesset affecting the judiciary, police and media. Matan Kahana, Eisenkot's candidate for Knesset speaker, is expected to be elected in a vote scheduled for November 17 — Arab-list representatives confirmed on Tuesday they would vote for him — and Avigdor Lieberman is set to head the Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee.
Negotiations continue behind the scenes to persuade one or two ultra-Orthodox lists to join a majority, possibly at the cost of softening the conscription-reform promise. Eisenkot has up to 42 days from his appointment on Sunday to form a government.
(Le Monde)
Source: lemonde.fr.

item.title: Trump nominated Palantir's security chief to run CISA — catch-up from Monday
item.description:
President Trump nominated Palantir chief information security officer Michael LoSapio on Monday to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, seeking to end a vacancy that has stretched nearly 22 months since Jen Easterly departed in January 2025.
LoSapio has been Palantir's CISO since September 2024, after leading its infrastructure and network security team since 2017. Trump's first nominee, Sean Plankey, withdrew in April after waiting more than a year.
The nomination faces a crowded lame-duck Senate calendar, and if LoSapio is not confirmed before the current Congress ends, Trump would have to nominate him again for consideration by the incoming Democratic majority. Acting director Nick Andersen has run the agency since February.
(Nextgov · Cybersecurity Dive)
Source: nextgov.com.

item.title: FTC expands Amazon Prime refunds — cap raised to $200, payments now automatic
item.description:
The FTC announced today that Amazon will accelerate and expand payments to eligible consumers under last year's $2.5 billion Prime settlement, after a federal court approved a joint FTC-Amazon motion this week. More consumers now qualify for refunds — including those who used between 11 and 20 Prime benefits in a year, who were excluded from earlier phases — the maximum payment cap rises from $51 to $200 total, and all future payments will be distributed automatically, with no claim or paperwork needed. As of September 2026, Amazon had issued more than $845 million in redress. The settlement resolved FTC allegations that Amazon enrolled millions in Prime without consent and made cancellation deliberately hard; Amazon did not admit liability. (Tourism TAS)
No fresh developments today in the Netanyahu trial, the Murdaugh retrial (next hearing November 13), or the FTC v. Amazon antitrust case (trial March 29, 2027).
Source: tourismtas.com.au.

item.title: Abu Dhabi talks end with a prisoner swap deal — but no ceasefire, and the grid attacks went on anyway
item.description:
The first three-way Ukraine talks in nine months ended in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday with one concrete result — a major prisoner-of-war release — and little else. US mediators were blunt about why: after two days of meetings there is, in Jared Kushner's words, "no trust right now between the sides," and the hardest question, territory, is still untouched. The fighting, meanwhile, did not pause for the talks: Russia hit six more Ukrainian power substations overnight, two of its missiles crossed into Moldovan airspace, and Ukrainian drones set fire to a Russian Baltic port — triggering shelter alerts across three NATO states.
The talks ran Tuesday and Wednesday in the Emirati capital, the first direct Russia-Ukraine negotiations with US participation since February. Ukraine's delegation was led by foreign intelligence chief Rustem Umerov, Russia's by Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, and the US side by special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. The first day lasted about four hours and focused largely on humanitarian questions — prisoner exchanges, the return of Ukrainian civilians held in Russia, and the fate of Ukrainian children taken to Russia. On the second day, the delegations agreed to a major release of prisoners of war — the scale discussed was 1,000-for-1,000, possibly 1,500 — but announced nothing else concrete, and issued no joint statement. Kushner said the talks had touched on territorial issues and that "these would be the hardest to resolve," adding that "some areas we see places where we can find compromises, other we need to have more discussions, but I think this was a very good step." Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia called the talks tough — Russia's delegation arrived with "strict directives" — but said they provided "good momentum" towards a solution before the end of the year. Medinsky said understanding had been reached on some issues, but was cool on the idea of European countries joining the talks.
What each side argues has not moved. Moscow wants the shape of a future European security order agreed before any ceasefire, and insists Ukraine surrender the parts of the Donbas it still holds before a peace deal can be struck. Kyiv wants the fighting to stop first and refuses to cede territory, proposing instead to freeze the conflict along the current front line; European capitals back that order, and a joint EU-US statement from Abu Dhabi said any settlement must respect Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity. A US official briefing reporters said both sides had privately shown some flexibility on territory and that security guarantees — possibly a defence commitment modelled on NATO's Article 5 — would be central, but neither government has said anything similar in public. Europe's place at the table was itself contested: European officials and NATO representatives met the US and Ukrainian teams in Abu Dhabi, but Russia's delegation declined to meet them. Kushner said he and Witkoff will travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet Putin — and raise broadening the talks to include the Europeans — then fly to Ireland to meet Zelenskyy.
For ordinary Ukrainians, the talks changed nothing overnight. Russia launched 163 strike drones and a Kh-59/69 guided missile at Ukraine overnight from Tuesday evening, including 91 jet-powered variants, according to the Ukrainian Air Force; 130 drones were shot down or neutralised. Six major electrical substations were hit in Vinnytsia, Kirovohrad, Zhytomyr and Cherkasy, Prime Minister Sergiy Koretskyi said, and grid operator Ukrenergo reported partial outages in eight regions. A heat supply facility in Kryvyi Rih was struck, cutting heating to residential buildings as winter sets in; a guided bomb damaged a school in Kherson, five apartment buildings were damaged in Kharkiv, and at least 14 people were injured. In the Odesa region, strikes on energy infrastructure left about 135,000 consumers without power, and an attack on a busy market killed three people, the regional governor said. Two Russian Banderol cruise missiles crossed into Moldovan airspace during the attack, Moldova's Defence Ministry reported, flying over villages in the south before re-entering Ukrainian airspace. And the war's spillover reached the Baltics on Wednesday: Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia briefly issued shelter alerts over unidentified drones, and Finland imposed temporary airspace and maritime curbs in the eastern Gulf of Finland — all later withdrawn — after Ukrainian drones hit Russia's Ust-Luga port area on the Baltic, setting it on fire and injuring three. Drone debris killed two people in Russia's Smolensk region, and one person was killed in a Ukrainian drone attack in Belgorod, according to local authorities.
In short: two days of Abu Dhabi talks produced a prisoner swap and not much else — no ceasefire, no movement on territory, and no trust, by the Americans' own account — while Russia kept hammering Ukraine's power grid and the war's drones kept straying into NATO airspace. The next step is Kushner and Witkoff in Moscow on Thursday, then with Zelenskyy in Ireland; whether the prisoner release actually happens, and whether the Europeans get a seat, are the things to watch.
Sources:
Source: duke.fm.

The fighting, meanwhile, did not pause for the talks: Russia hit six more Ukrainian power substations overnight, two of its missiles crossed into Moldovan airspace, and Ukrainian drones set fire to a Russian Baltic port — triggering shelter alerts across three NATO states.

The talks ran Tuesday and Wednesday in the Emirati capital, the first direct Russia-Ukraine negotiations with US participation since February. Ukraine's delegation was led by foreign intelligence chief Rustem Umerov, Russia's by Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, and the US side by special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. The first day lasted about four hours and focused largely on humanitarian questions — prisoner exchanges, the return of Ukrainian civilians held in Russia, and the fate of Ukrainian children taken to Russia. On the second day, the delegations agreed to a major release of prisoners of war — the scale discussed was 1,000-for-1,000, possibly 1,500 — but announced nothing else concrete, and issued no joint statement. Kushner said the talks had touched on territorial issues and that "these would be the hardest to resolve," adding that "some areas we see places where we can find compromises, other we need to have more discussions, but I think this was a very good step." Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia called the talks tough — Russia's delegation arrived with "strict directives" — but said they provided "good momentum" towards a solution before the end of the year. Medinsky said understanding had been reached on some issues, but was cool on the idea of European countries joining the talks.

What each side argues has not moved. Moscow wants the shape of a future European security order agreed before any ceasefire, and insists Ukraine surrender the parts of the Donbas it still holds before a peace deal can be struck. Kyiv wants the fighting to stop first and refuses to cede territory, proposing instead to freeze the conflict along the current front line; European capitals back that order, and a joint EU-US statement from Abu Dhabi said any settlement must respect Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity. A US official briefing reporters said both sides had privately shown some flexibility on territory and that security guarantees — possibly a defence commitment modelled on NATO's Article 5 — would be central, but neither government has said anything similar in public. Europe's place at the table was itself contested: European officials and NATO representatives met the US and Ukrainian teams in Abu Dhabi, but Russia's delegation declined to meet them. Kushner said he and Witkoff will travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet Putin — and raise broadening the talks to include the Europeans — then fly to Ireland to meet Zelenskyy.

For ordinary Ukrainians, the talks changed nothing overnight. Russia launched 163 strike drones and a Kh-59/69 guided missile at Ukraine overnight from Tuesday evening, including 91 jet-powered variants, according to the Ukrainian Air Force; 130 drones were shot down or neutralised. Six major electrical substations were hit in Vinnytsia, Kirovohrad, Zhytomyr and Cherkasy, Prime Minister Sergiy Koretskyi said, and grid operator Ukrenergo reported partial outages in eight regions. A heat supply facility in Kryvyi Rih was struck, cutting heating to residential buildings as winter sets in; a guided bomb damaged a school in Kherson, five apartment buildings were damaged in Kharkiv, and at least 14 people were injured. In the Odesa region, strikes on energy infrastructure left about 135,000 consumers without power, and an attack on a busy market killed three people, the regional governor said. Two Russian Banderol cruise missiles crossed into Moldovan airspace during the attack, Moldova's Defence Ministry reported, flying over villages in the south before re-entering Ukrainian airspace. And the war's spillover reached the Baltics on Wednesday: Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia briefly issued shelter alerts over unidentified drones, and Finland imposed temporary airspace and maritime curbs in the eastern Gulf of Finland — all later withdrawn — after Ukrainian drones hit Russia's Ust-Luga port area on the Baltic, setting it on fire and injuring three. Drone debris killed two people in Russia's Smolensk region, and one person was killed in a Ukrainian drone attack in Belgorod, according to local authorities.

In short: two days of Abu Dhabi talks produced a prisoner swap and not much else — no ceasefire, no movement on territory, and no trust, by the Americans' own account — while Russia kept hammering Ukraine's power grid and the war's drones kept straying into NATO airspace. The next step is Kushner and Witkoff in Moscow on Thursday, then with Zelenskyy in Ireland; whether the prisoner release actually happens, and whether the Europeans get a seat, are the things to watch.

item.title: Iran and the US are telling two different stories about the same war
item.description:
Washington and Tehran cannot agree on whether they are even talking — and that disagreement is now the story. On Tuesday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared that Operation Epic Fury, the US-Israel war on Iran that began February 28, "is concluded" because its objectives were achieved, and President Trump paused Project Freedom, the naval mission to guide stranded ships out of the Strait of Hormuz, saying "great progress" had been made toward a final agreement. On the same day, Iran's top security official, Mohsen Rezaei, went on Lebanon's Al Mayadeen TV and called reports of negotiations "a pure lie," said the Strait of Hormuz "will not reopen until the US meets Tehran's seven conditions," and insisted Washington was talking up talks to ease economic pressure and bring down oil prices.
The details of the two accounts barely overlap. According to Rubio, speaking at a White House briefing on Tuesday, "The Operation Epic Fury is concluded. We achieved the objectives of that operation," and "we're not cheering for an additional situation to occur. We would prefer the path of peace." Trump announced the Project Freedom pause on Truth Social on Tuesday, saying it was "based on the request" of Pakistan and other countries and that the blockade would stay in full force while the two sides try to finalise a deal. Reuters and Axios reported the US has floated a one-page memorandum of understanding to formally end hostilities and open a 30-day window for detailed negotiations — under it, Iran would commit to a moratorium on nuclear enrichment while the US lifts sanctions and releases frozen Iranian funds, and both sides allow transit through Hormuz. But Trump struck a more conditional note in a social media post on Wednesday, writing that Epic Fury would "be at an end" only if Iran "agrees to give what has been agreed to" — and "if they don't agree, the bombing starts, and it will be, sadly, at a much higher level and intensity than it was before." The IRGC navy said on Wednesday that safe transit through the strait would be ensured, and the US said it had evacuated 22 crew members held on an Iranian container vessel to Pakistan as a confidence-building measure.
Tehran's version is the opposite. Rezaei said Iran is still waiting for an explicit US response to its seven conditions — which include lifting sanctions and the US naval blockade and ending the fighting on all fronts, especially Israeli attacks on Lebanon — and that the initial US response was "insufficient and deceptive." Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told state news agency IRNA that "the conflict with Iran will not be resolved through military means, nor by intensifying sanctions," and that Hormuz could reopen within two days if the demands are met. Both Rezaei and Araghchi rejected reports of a meeting with US Vice President JD Vance as baseless. Meanwhile the attacks on shipping have not stopped: the IRGC claimed three oil tankers caught fire on Tuesday after striking naval mines on an "unauthorised route" in the eastern strait, and the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency confirmed reports of two tanker incidents, including one struck by an unknown projectile northeast of Oman's Lima village. Those claims are unverified — no vessel names or casualties have been given — but maritime monitors count at least 37 ships attacked in and near Hormuz in October, the highest monthly total since the war began, with 10 more so far in November. Iran's Fars news agency also claimed a US warship was hit with two missiles near Jask on Monday; the US military denied it, and no independent evidence has confirmed it. CENTCOM says US forces have helped move more than 900 million barrels of crude through the strait since early May.
For ordinary people, the gap between the two stories is the danger: oil is the tell. Brent crude rose about 0.9% to $92.83 a barrel on the tanker attacks, while the International Maritime Organization estimates up to 20,000 seafarers are stranded aboard roughly 2,000 vessels in the Gulf. If the US account is right and a deal is near, shipping and fuel prices could ease quickly; if Iran's account is right and there is no deal, the strait stays shut, the mines stay in the water, and the blockade — which Rubio called a defensive measure and Iran calls an act of war — keeps squeezing both sides.
In short: the US says its war on Iran is over and a deal is close; Iran says there are no talks at all and the strait stays shut until its seven conditions are met. Both can't be right. The test is whether the one-page memorandum Axios described actually gets signed — or whether Trump's warning of resumed bombing "at a much higher level" is what comes next.
Sources:
Source: 234radio.com.

item.title: Nvidia: today is the House deadline — and the pressure on Huang is now coming from inside his own party
item.description:
Today, Wednesday, is the deadline House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast set for Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to answer a request for a closed-door briefing on November 18 about his interactions with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom US agencies allege was recruited by Chinese intelligence. Mast told ABC News on Tuesday he is "absolutely" prepared to subpoena Huang if he does not respond by today. No subpoena has been issued, and Nvidia has not publicly said whether Huang will attend. The pressure is no longer just from the House: on Tuesday evening, Senator Kevin Cramer of North Dakota, a senior Republican on the Senate Banking Committee, became the first sitting senator to call on Huang to step down, telling POLITICO "the potential for extortion is so tremendous that something as sensitive as Nvidia chips, I just think he's got to go." And on Wednesday morning, Baird downgraded Nvidia to Neutral from Outperform and slashed its price target to $200 from $500, citing less visibility into 2027 data-centre forecasts, cooling hyperscaler spending, and uncertainty over whether Huang stays CEO through 2027.
The board's own investigation is still running. Nvidia's independent directors hired former acting US Attorney Joon H. Kim and the firm Wachtell Lipton on Tuesday to lead it, after the board opened the inquiry on Sunday, November 8, into reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The board has said it has "no reason to believe" national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but called that a preliminary position, and Huang remains CEO with the board's stated confidence. Huang admitted in a staff email on Sunday that he was unfaithful to his wife and apologised; neither his message nor the board's statement addressed the chip sales at the centre of the reporting.
The story has widened well beyond the affair, and several developments from the last two days had not been reported in this brief before. Nvidia and Huang were sued on Monday in a proposed securities class action accusing them of defrauding shareholders by concealing Huang's ties to a suspected Chinese spy, Reuters reported; Trump said he had spoken with Huang and that the FBI is "looking into it." The Information reported on Tuesday, citing two people who know Alice Huang, that the relationship helped enable at least $7.5 billion of Nvidia chip shipments, with ties dating back to 2023 — Reuters said it could not independently verify that report. A New York Times investigation published Monday found the Commerce Department cleared roughly two dozen Chinese companies to buy or handle Nvidia's H200 chips — including Baidu, BYD, Alibaba, Tencent and ByteDance — but two approved server assemblers had empty offices at their listed addresses, and several approved firms have ownership ties to US-blacklisted companies or Chinese military suppliers. Bloomberg reported that Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter called Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler in late summer 2025 about a probe into suspected chip smuggling by Singapore-based Megaspeed, and that Nvidia's inventory tallies given to the US government undercounted chips sold to Megaspeed via hardware partners by about 50,000 units. Bank of America removed Nvidia, Micron and Lam Research from its US 1 List of top stock picks.
What each side argues is now a three-way fight. Lawmakers — Mast, Moolenaar and Crawford in the House, Cramer in the Senate, and Democratic leaders Schumer and Jeffries — say the reported relationship raises a national-security question about who has access to the world's most important AI chips, and want answers under oath or in a closed briefing. Nvidia's position is that its own checks found no evidence its chips were diverted, that Megaspeed denies diverting them, and that the board's independent inquiry will examine all available information. Wall Street is split: Baird sees a leadership overhang and a cooling data-centre cycle, while the stock bounced about 5% in premarket trading on Wednesday after closing Tuesday at $168.89, down 5.5% — a sector-wide lift led by CoreWeave, up about 17% after beating earnings. The scale of the slide is stark either way: Microsoft passed Nvidia in market value intraday on Monday, about $4.035 trillion to $4.032 trillion, the first time since June 2025, and Nvidia's value is down roughly $1.7 trillion since October 6.
In short: today is the day Huang has to answer Congress — subpoena threat on the table, a Republican senator now calling for his resignation, a Wall Street downgrade, and a securities lawsuit — while the board's investigation runs and Nvidia reports earnings on November 17, the day before the requested briefing. The allegations that secrets were compromised remain unproven, but the political and market pressure is now coming from every direction at once.
Sources:
Source: cosanalyst.com.

item.title: Houthi/Saudi — missiles fired at Riyadh again on Wednesday morning
item.description:
The Saudi-led coalition intercepted missiles fired at Riyadh on Wednesday morning, according to FirstSquawk — three cruise missiles, per one report, two per another — with no casualties reported.
The reports are single-source and the count differs, so treat this as developing; it follows Monday night's interception of three Houthi missiles (a ballistic and a cruise missile over Riyadh, plus a ballistic missile over the south). No Houthi claim of responsibility had been published by brief time.
(CryptoBriefing · Internet Zarada)
Source: cryptobriefing.com.

item.title: Khor Mor — production reported restored, but reports conflict
item.description:
Dana Gas confirmed on Wednesday that production at the Khor Mor gas field in Iraqi Kurdistan is back to normal after Sunday night's drone attack, and the Kurdistan Regional Government said 24/7 electricity supply was restored on Sunday.
The strike had cut 2,500–2,800 MW — roughly 70–80% of the region's power. One report this morning still described the field as shut and gas not resumed, so the resumption is not yet unanimous in the reporting — but the operator's own confirmation is the stronger signal.
No group has claimed responsibility for the attack. (Kurdistan Chronicle · Tiger Brokers · Hathalyoum)
Source: kurdistanchronicle.com.

item.title: Google's November Pixel Drop is out — Pixel Tag goes on sale today
item.description:
Google's November Pixel Drop began rolling out on November 10, and the Pixel Tag — Google's AirTag rival, first shown in August — goes on sale today, November 11, at $29.99 for one or $99.99 for a four-pack, with ultra-wideband guidance through Android's Find Hub network.
The drop brings Gemini Intelligence to Pixel 10 phones, including Rambler, a voice-typing tool that strips fillers and formats messages, plus Gemini calling on Pixel 10 and 11 (US and English first) and Pixel Search on every Pixel back to the Pixel 6. Google Fi adds automatic switching between two 5G networks and encrypted Wi-Fi.
This is a feature rollout, not a new phone — the Pixel Tag is the only new hardware, and it was announced three months ago. (Google blog · TechDogs)
Source: blog.google.

item.title: Microsoft's November Patch Tuesday fixed about 1,094 flaws — only one confirmed exploited
item.description:
Microsoft's November Patch Tuesday addressed roughly 1,094 vulnerabilities, with 63 rated Critical — the second straight month over 1,000.
The only one confirmed exploited is the Outlook zero-day already in CISA's KEV catalog (CVE-2026-124194, an NTLM hash leak, federal deadline November 24). No new KEV additions were published overnight; the November 9 four (SSHole, GPUStack, FreeSWITCH, IBM Aspera Faspex) carry a federal deadline of tomorrow, November 12, and the Barracuda pair is due Friday, November 13.
(Rod Trent / Security Check-in)
Source: rodtrent.substack.com.

item.title: Abu Dhabi talks end day one with warm words and no deal
item.description:
The first three-way talks between Ukraine, Russia, and the United States in nine months wrapped up their first day in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday with both sides talking past each other in public: Ukraine's president called the session "constructive and quite substantive," while Russia said nothing at all, and no joint statement was issued. The delegations meet again on Wednesday.
The talks ran about four hours inside the Emirates Palace hotel, with a roughly 40-minute break, according to Le Monde. They opened with separate meetings between Ukraine's team and European and American officials, followed by the trilateral session itself. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner led the American side; Rustem Umerov led Ukraine's delegation, with presidential office chief Kyrylo Budanov also at the table. Notably, Budanov sat across from Dmitry Minaev, the FSB counterintelligence chief whom Ukrainian intelligence says orchestrated a 2019 assassination attempt against him — a detail Le Monde reads as Moscow signaling dominance rather than compromise.
The substance, as far as either side has described it: Zelensky said on X after being briefed by his team that the talks covered prisoner releases, security guarantees for Ukraine, and "mechanisms to block any recurrence of the war." Speaking to reporters in Copenhagen later in the evening, he said a prisoner swap of 1,000 for 1,000 — possibly 1,500 for 1,500 — was discussed, and that Kyiv has offered a ceasefire at sea and on energy sites and is waiting for Moscow to answer. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was not in Abu Dhabi, called the first day "very productive." Zelensky said his team has "clear instructions" for day two, when de-escalation, energy, the Black Sea, the prisoner exchange, and a possible leaders' meeting are on the agenda.
What each side argues: Kyiv and its European allies insist on a ceasefire first, then security guarantees — a joint European-American statement on Tuesday put that in writing, insisting on respect for Ukraine's "sovereignty and territorial integrity." Russia, per Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, will not agree to an immediate ceasefire without knowing what comes after it, and the Kremlin continues to demand Ukraine cede the Donbas, which it controls roughly 80–85% of. The NY Post notes Russia has been unable to take the rest of the Donetsk fortress belt by force, while Ukraine fears surrendering it would open the way for a future advance. item.content:encoded:
The first three-way talks between Ukraine, Russia, and the United States in nine months wrapped up their first day in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday with both sides talking past each other in public: Ukraine's president called the session "constructive and quite substantive," while Russia said nothing at all, and no joint statement was issued. The delegations meet again on Wednesday.

The talks ran about four hours inside the Emirates Palace hotel, with a roughly 40-minute break, according to Le Monde. They opened with separate meetings between Ukraine's team and European and American officials, followed by the trilateral session itself. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner led the American side; Rustem Umerov led Ukraine's delegation, with presidential office chief Kyrylo Budanov also at the table. Notably, Budanov sat across from Dmitry Minaev, the FSB counterintelligence chief whom Ukrainian intelligence says orchestrated a 2019 assassination attempt against him — a detail Le Monde reads as Moscow signaling dominance rather than compromise.

The substance, as far as either side has described it: Zelensky said on X after being briefed by his team that the talks covered prisoner releases, security guarantees for Ukraine, and "mechanisms to block any recurrence of the war." Speaking to reporters in Copenhagen later in the evening, he said a prisoner swap of 1,000 for 1,000 — possibly 1,500 for 1,500 — was discussed, and that Kyiv has offered a ceasefire at sea and on energy sites and is waiting for Moscow to answer. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was not in Abu Dhabi, called the first day "very productive." Zelensky said his team has "clear instructions" for day two, when de-escalation, energy, the Black Sea, the prisoner exchange, and a possible leaders' meeting are on the agenda.

What each side argues: Kyiv and its European allies insist on a ceasefire first, then security guarantees — a joint European-American statement on Tuesday put that in writing, insisting on respect for Ukraine's "sovereignty and territorial integrity." Russia, per Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, will not agree to an immediate ceasefire without knowing what comes after it, and the Kremlin continues to demand Ukraine cede the Donbas, which it controls roughly 80–85% of. The NY Post notes Russia has been unable to take the rest of the Donetsk fortress belt by force, while Ukraine fears surrendering it would open the way for a future advance. Le Monde reports the U.S. envoys have been floating a new European security architecture that would accommodate Russia — language that echoes Putin's goal of rolling back NATO's reach — and that the E3 (Germany, France, and the U.K.) traveled to Abu Dhabi to make sure Witkoff and Kushner didn't offer further concessions for a hasty settlement. Trump, per Rubio, has made resolving the war "a priority" after the November 3 midterm defeat, with a new Congress hostile to his administration taking office in January.

For ordinary Ukrainians, the talks changed nothing on the ground: Russia's grid campaign continued into a second night, with 850,000+ people without power in the east as of the evening brief, and scheduled outages are set to last at least through Monday as repair crews work through the damage. The war is set to mark its five-year anniversary next February.

In short: day one produced a meeting, not a breakthrough — a prisoner swap and a sea-and-energy ceasefire are on the table, the ceasefire-first question is still unresolved, and the real test is whether Wednesday's session moves past warm adjectives.

item.title: IRGC claims third tanker struck a mine in the Strait of Hormuz
item.description:
Iran's Revolutionary Guard Navy said Tuesday afternoon that a third oil tanker exploded after hitting a naval mine on an "unauthorized route" in the eastern Strait of Hormuz, and was left burning. Earlier Tuesday it said two other tankers were left ablaze after explosions on the same route — one described as a supertanker that struck a mine, the other immobilized under U.S. military escort. The IRGC named no tanker, flag, or crew in any of the three claims, gave no casualty figures, and none of the incidents has been independently confirmed. The IRGC also claims U.S. coastal radar and navigation systems south of the strait were destroyed, raising the risk for ships on unauthorized lanes. The U.S. answer to Iran's seven conditions is still due, and Tehran denied a report of an $8B frozen-assets-for-Hormuz deal. Brent traded around $91 a barrel Tuesday, WTI around $85.
Sources:
Source: presstv.co.uk.

item.title: Six new CISA KEV entries, November 10 — patch now
item.description:
CISA added six vulnerabilities with evidence of active exploitation: an Outlook flaw (CVE-2026-124194) that leaks NTLM hashes, a Chrome zero-day (CVE-2026-125350, use-after-free, fixed in Chrome 157.0.8103.50), two Barracuda flaws (CVE-2026-116606, CVSS 9.3 pre-auth auth bypass in Email Security Gateway, and CVE-2026-111560, CVSS 8.6 OS command injection across six Barracuda products — Barracuda confirmed exploitation hitting a small number of orgs on Nov 9), Cisco BroadWorks CVE-2026-20320, and Openwave Messaging Webtop CVE-2026-111793. Federal deadlines: Barracuda flaws by November 13, the other four by November 24. This supersedes the evening brief's "no new KEV additions" note — the additions landed after it.
Sources:
Source: securityonline.info.

item.title: Anthropic's IPO roadshow is officially underway
item.description:
Reuters reports the company launched the roadshow Tuesday, aiming to raise as much as $64.4 billion by selling 825 million shares at $70–$78, targeting a valuation of up to $1.02 trillion — $1.4 trillion on a fully diluted basis. A separate $26 billion private placement is lined up with cornerstone investors including Google ($10B), Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft ($1B) and TSMC. Reuters calculates Amazon's and Google's existing Anthropic stakes could be worth a combined $411 billion at the top of the range. Pricing is expected next week. Separately on Tuesday, Anthropic announced Claude Meetings, bringing Claude into Google Meet calls as a visible participant for Team and Enterprise customers. The earlier $69.3B figure from Monday's draft filing was retracted by the company as inaccurate.
Sources:
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Nvidia's board retained Joon H. Kim of Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to lead the independent investigation into CEO Jensen Huang
item.description:
Kim is a former acting U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York who previously co-led the investigation into former New York governor Andrew Cuomo. The board announced the probe Sunday after reports Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort through a relationship with a woman U.S. officials allege has Chinese intelligence links; Huang admitted infidelity in an email to staff. The board says it has "no reason to believe" national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that is a preliminary position, not a finding. Huang stays on as CEO during the investigation. Nvidia shares fell 4.2% Tuesday to $171.16. The House briefing answer is due Wednesday, November 11; earnings are November 17.
Sources:
Source: nypost.com.

item.title: Russia is trying to "divide Ukraine along the Dnipro," Zelensky says, as the grid campaign rolls into a second night
item.description:
Russia kept hitting Ukraine's power grid through a second night of strikes while the first day of three-way talks in Abu Dhabi ended with no movement — and President Volodymyr Zelensky used his evening address to frame the campaign as an attempt to split the country in two along the Dnipro River. More than 850,000 people were left without power in the east, and the IAEA confirmed a drone strike killed a worker at the occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant on Monday.
The overnight strikes into Tuesday morning — 162 drones and a ballistic missile hitting five major substations across 10 regions, killing two people in Vinnytsia — were covered in this morning's brief. What changed during the day is the scale of the damage and the framing. Energy company DTEK said the strikes damaged key equipment in Dnipropetrovsk region and cut power to large parts of Dnipro and Kamianske in the evening, leaving more than 600,000 people without electricity there and another 250,000 in Kharkiv region, according to reports from Nexus Europa citing DTEK. State grid operator Ukrenergo said energy infrastructure was hit in eight regions and kept scheduled blackouts in force into the evening, with hourly outage schedules for households and capacity limits for industry. In Poltava, strikes also knocked out power and water and hit an enterprise in Kremenchuk.
Caption: High-voltage transmission towers — the power grid Russia has been hammering in its renewed air campaign as winter approaches, with substations in Poltava, Dnipropetrovsk, Vinnytsia and Kirovohrad hit overnight.
Zelensky said in his evening televised address that Russian forces are "trying to divide Ukraine along the Dnipro River" by striking bridges and the power grid, and that the strikes aimed to "make life as difficult as possible for people, for our cities and villages." The Financial Times reported he told European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen the same, and a Ukrainian official told the paper Kyiv believes Russia plans to disrupt transport and ammunition shipments across the river and cut the flow of electricity from Ukraine's west to its east. Russia began heavily striking bridges across the Dnipro in Kyiv in October. Moscow, for its part, confirmed it launched attacks against Ukrainian energy facilities and a commercial container ship, and Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov repeated after day one in Abu Dhabi that Russia will not agree to an immediate ceasefire without knowing what comes next — the security-order-first position covered in this morning's brief. Ukraine hit back as well: Moscow-appointed officials in occupied Luhansk said Ukrainian drones knocked out power across the city and nearby towns, and reported at least three dead and four injured in drone attacks at other frontline points — a claim from Russian-appointed authorities, not independently verified.
The human cost keeps mounting at the edges of the campaign. The IAEA reported that drones killed a Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant employee and a worker at the Zaporizhzhia thermal power plant on Monday, November 9. The occupied Zaporizhzhia plant itself ran on emergency diesel generators for about ten hours on Sunday after losing its only external power line — its 27th blackout of the war — before power was restored. For ordinary Ukrainians, this is the fifth winter of the war, and the grid attacks are landing as temperatures fall toward freezing: homes across six regions woke up without power, and scheduled blackouts are now a daily routine.
In short: day one of the Abu Dhabi talks ended with the same split as it began — Moscow wants a security order agreed before a ceasefire, Kyiv wants the ceasefire first — while Russia's grid campaign rolled into a second night, leaving 850,000+ people without power in the east, and Zelensky framed the strikes as an attempt to divide Ukraine along the Dnipro. Day two of the talks is Wednesday.
Sources:
Source: tbsnews.net.

item.title: France formally blames Iran's Revolutionary Guard for the supermarket freezer cyberattack
item.description:
France on Monday formally accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of carrying out the cyberattack that sabotaged refrigeration systems at roughly 700 sites across France last month — the first time Paris has directly blamed Tehran for a cyberattack — and named the unit and three men it holds responsible. Paris prosecutors have opened a judicial investigation and requested international arrest warrants, and France summoned Iran's ambassador on Tuesday.
The attack, on the night of October 11–12, hit supermarkets — Carrefour, Intermarché, Netto, Coopérative U and Monoprix among them — plus a slaughterhouse, food processing plants and hydroelectric facilities. According to a five-page report from France's Cyber Crisis Coordination Centre, which brings together the national cybersecurity agency ANSSI, the military's cyber command and the DGSE and DGSI intelligence services, the hackers overrode digital thermostats and forced defrost cycles, driving temperatures from as low as minus 16.6 degrees Fahrenheit to above 122 degrees Fahrenheit. At least 15 fires broke out. The same hackers also probed Schneider Electric controllers at several small French hydroelectric plants, with moderate disruption. The report names the unit as Shahid Kaveh, an offensive cyber unit of the IRGC's electronic and cyber centre, and names its head, Hamid Reza Lashgarian, 65, along with Mahdi Lashgarian, 37, and Reza Salarvand, 35, as its commanders. Investigators linked the attack to the unit through Farsi-language traces in the code and infrastructure, matching tactics and tooling from earlier Shahid Kaveh hacks, IP addresses in Iran, and publicity of the attacks on propaganda channels linked to the unit, such as CyberAv3ngers. The French report says the hackers worked through numerous front groups masquerading as vigilante hackers, including CyberAv3ngers and the Cyber Isnaad Front.
Caption: A shopper in front of supermarket freezer cabinets — the kind of refrigeration systems hackers seized control of at roughly 700 French sites on October 11–12, forcing defrost cycles that spoiled food and started at least 15 fires.
France's position is that this was a state-ordered attack of "unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggressiveness," in Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot's words, and it will seek European sanctions against those responsible. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc's Foreign Affairs Council will take up the incidents on November 16 and called for a strong response if Iran is confirmed responsible. Iran has not formally responded to the attribution, and Tehran routinely denies carrying out malicious cyber operations. Not everyone is convinced: UK cyber security specialist Peter Bassill told The Grocer there is "no evidence factual or anecdotal that points to Iran being the culprit," and France has not published the underlying intelligence. The unit is already well known to US agencies — the Defense Department, FBI and NSA identified Shahid Kaveh earlier this year as another name for CyberAv3ngers, blamed for disrupting operational technology at US water utilities, and the State Department has offered up to $10 million for information on IRGC officials behind the group's 2023 attacks on US water utilities. Iran is also a suspect in refrigeration failures at six or more US military commissaries in August, which Pentagon investigators are treating as a suspected cyberattack; Microsoft had privately linked Iran to the French sabotage weeks before Paris went public, Reuters reported.
For ordinary people, this was an attack on food, not on data: fridges and freezers warming to over 122 degrees means spoiled stock, shuttered shops and, in the worst cases, fires in buildings full of shoppers. It also shows how exposed the everyday systems behind the food supply are — the same Danish Danfoss controllers that run supermarket refrigeration are widely deployed, and the attack needed no exotic capability, just access to poorly protected remote management. Proofpoint researcher Saher Naumaan told Reuters the sabotage showed less about Iran's skill than about how exposed such systems are.
In short: France has put a name and three faces on the October freezer attacks — Iran's IRGC cyber unit Shahid Kaveh — and is pursuing arrest warrants and EU sanctions, while Iran has not formally responded and at least some independent experts question the attribution. The EU takes it up on November 16, and the same unit is already suspected in similar refrigeration failures at US military grocery stores in August.
Sources:
Source: sofx.com.

item.title: Ex-cop Matthew Farwell convicted of killing pregnant Sandra Birchmore
item.description:
A federal jury in Boston convicted former Stoughton police officer Matthew Farwell on Tuesday of killing Sandra Birchmore, 23 and pregnant, and causing the death of her unborn child — a verdict that came a day after the same jury told the judge it was deadlocked. Farwell, 41, faces a mandatory life sentence when he is sentenced on February 3, 2027.
The jury of eight men and four women deliberated for roughly 14 hours over two days. On Monday afternoon they sent Chief U.S. District Judge Denise Casper a note saying they were deadlocked and did not expect that to change; the judge sent them home and told them Tuesday morning to keep working. At around 2 p.m. on Tuesday they returned guilty verdicts on both counts: killing a witness or victim under 18 U.S.C. § 1512(a)(1)(C), and causing the death of a child in utero under 18 U.S.C. § 1841. People could be heard crying in the courtroom gallery and Birchmore's family and friends hugged each other after the verdict was read, according to WCVB, and U.S. Attorney Leah Foley said afterward: "Despite Mr. Farwell's attempt to silence Sandra Birchmore, today her story is told… Justice has indeed been served."
Caption: Matthew Farwell, 41, in a photo provided by the Stoughton, Massachusetts, Police Department. A federal jury convicted him Tuesday of killing Sandra Birchmore and her unborn child; he faces a mandatory life sentence at sentencing on February 3, 2027.
Prosecutors said Farwell strangled Birchmore in her Canton apartment on February 1, 2021, and staged the scene to look like a suicide by hanging, to stop her from exposing a sexual relationship that began when she was 15 and he was a 27-year-old officer who met her through the Stoughton Police Explorers program for kids. In closing, prosecutor Brian Fogerty argued Farwell killed her to "clean up his mess" because he was about to be "exposed" — Birchmore had told him she was ready to come forward, and he killed her the day before his wife gave birth to their third child. The defense, led by attorney Kimberly Stevens, did not deny the affair but argued Birchmore took her own life the same night Farwell told her he was breaking things off, saying she had "built a fantasy world" around marrying him. Prosecutors also revealed at trial that DNA showed the fetus belonged to another man, not Farwell, and that Birchmore had become pregnant in December 2020 after demanding Farwell have a child with her or she would expose the affair. Her death was initially ruled a suicide by state investigators; the medical examiner later changed the manner of death to undetermined, and federal prosecutors took up the case, arresting Farwell in August 2024, more than three years later.
For Birchmore's family, the verdict ends nearly six years of waiting since a death first dismissed as suicide. For Stoughton and Massachusetts policing, it closes a case that exposed how a police officer used a youth program to groom a child — and how the original investigation, which prosecutors criticized for unrecorded interviews and missing warrants, failed her. Farwell has been in custody since his 2024 arrest.
In short: after a near four-week trial and a Monday deadlock that looked like it might end in a mistrial, the jury convicted Matthew Farwell on both counts Tuesday afternoon. He faces mandatory life in prison at sentencing on February 3, 2027.

item.title: Houthis claim four more strikes on Saudi Arabia
item.description:
The Houthis announced on Tuesday that they carried out four strikes against Saudi Arabia — hitting King Khalid International Airport, the financial district in Riyadh, a facility owned by Aramco, and Saudi troop concentrations — and warned they will keep operating deep inside Saudi territory.
They said the attacks were a response to a recent Saudi strike on a market in Taiz in southern Yemen. The claim came a day after the coalition said it intercepted three Houthi missiles overnight (a ballistic and a cruise missile toward Riyadh, another ballistic missile toward the south) plus a drone over the Eastern Province, with no casualties reported.
The Houthis also said on Tuesday they attacked the East-West oil pipeline in Riyadh Province — while denying the Saudi assertion that they hit the pipeline in the Medina region on Monday, where the Saudis reported a limited fire that was extinguished with no casualties and no effect on operations. Riyadh's deputy governor inspected the damaged Aramco administrative building in the capital on Tuesday and said the attack showed the Houthis targeting civilian facilities.
(AzerNews · SRN News (Reuters) · TBS News)
Source: azernews.az.

item.title: Iran — Araghchi presses the US to meet Tehran's demands; no answer yet
item.description:
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Tuesday that "the conflict with Iran will not be resolved through military means, nor by intensifying sanctions," and that the only solution is diplomacy that addresses Iran's demands in its two-day proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz — ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the US counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Tehran also denied reports, carried by Fars News Agency, that it had agreed to negotiate reopening the strait in exchange for $8 billion in frozen assets, calling them completely false. The US answer to Tehran's proposal was still due today, with Qatari officials in Tehran; Reuters reported oil flows through the strait have recovered to around 80 percent of prewar levels.
The split inside Tehran continues — President Pezeshkian talking negotiation, security chief Rezaei insisting the US "submit to the seven conditions." (Arab News · Stockbiz / Fars · IranWire)
Source: arabnews-pk.maestronewsroom.com.

item.title: Israel — Knesset sworn in; speaker vote set for November 17
item.description:
Israel's 26th Knesset was sworn in on Tuesday afternoon, with 46 first-time members, and the opposition bloc submitted the signatures of 67 lawmakers to replace Speaker Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally, with Matan Kahana of Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party.
Ohana said he has scheduled the vote for Tuesday, November 17, at 4 p.m. The Eisenkot bloc also filed bills on its first day for a state commission of inquiry into the October 7, 2023 attack, a limit on a prime minister's time in office, and a repeal of the judicial overhaul — and agreed Avigdor Lieberman will chair the Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee.
Netanyahu, still caretaker prime minister, used the ceremony to attack the government Eisenkot is trying to form. Eisenkot has 28 days from November 8 to form a government, with a possible 14-day extension.
(Silent Dossier · The Insight International · Hathalyoum / Anadolu)
Source: silentdossier.com.

item.title: FTC v. Amazon — economics hearing: judge presses the FTC on consumer harm
item.description:
At Tuesday's economics hearing in the FTC's antitrust case against Amazon, Judge John Chun pressed the FTC on what consumer harm it is actually trying to prove — lower quality, higher prices — and on whether it can show what the market would have looked like without Amazon's conduct.
The FTC said it is challenging a course of conduct that keeps rivals from competing, which indirectly raises prices for sellers and shoppers, but conceded it cannot quantify a "but-for world." The judge also noted the FTC's case mirrors a consumer case he oversees, Hogan v.
Amazon, which he said "is going pretty poorly." Separately, Milan prosecutors have closed an investigation into Amazon over the circulation of 1,519,613 non-EU goods in Italy's customs territory, with €3,549,612 in allegedly unpaid taxes and duties covering 2021 to March 2026 — the next step would be a request to send the case to trial.
The FTC's Prime "dark patterns" jury trial continues in Seattle. (Typefully · EL7)
Source: typefully.com.

item.title: Cyber — "SSHole" exploitation still climbing; KEV deadline is Thursday
item.description:
Previdian's sensors have now logged 26 exploitation attempts against OpenSSH's "SSHole" flaw (CVE-2026-123158) from 17 unique attacker IPs across 12 countries, first observed November 6 and last observed today, November 10.
The Hacker News reported on the same CISA batch today — four flaws added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Monday (GPUStack, SignalWire FreeSWITCH, OpenSSH "SSHole," IBM Aspera Faspex), all with a federal remediation deadline of Thursday, November 12. No new KEV additions today.
(Previdian · Tech Insider)
Source: previdian.com.

item.title: Russia pounds Ukraine's grid as Abu Dhabi talks open — and end day one still split
item.description:
Russia hit Ukraine's power grid again overnight, killing two people and knocking out substations across the country, on the very morning Russian, Ukrainian and American negotiators sat down in Abu Dhabi for their first three-way talks since February. By the end of day one, the positions were exactly where they started: Moscow wants the shape of a future European security order agreed before any ceasefire, Kyiv wants the shooting to stop first, and the land question hasn't moved at all.
Russian forces struck 10 Ukrainian regions overnight, hitting five major electrical substations that move power between regions — in Poltava, Dnipropetrovsk, Vinnytsia and Kirovohrad — according to Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretskyi. Two people were killed in the Vinnytsia region. State grid operator Ukrenergo said energy infrastructure was hit in eight regions overnight and into the morning, leaving homes without power in six, including Kyiv, Kharkiv and Dnipropetrovsk. Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 162 drones and a ballistic missile overnight. The Guardian's live blog, citing the Kyiv Independent, reported at least nine people killed and 39 injured across Ukraine over the past day. Russia's defence ministry said its forces shot down 155 Ukrainian drones overnight over eight Russian regions and Crimea, and said it struck cargo vessels and a tanker in the Black Sea, including a ship east of Odesa.
The talks themselves opened in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday with the US envoy Jared Kushner telling reporters that almost daily contacts with both sides had "narrowed the gaps" and that the Americans had "some good ideas on how to bridge it" — but he stopped short of promising a settlement. The Russian delegation is led by Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, Ukraine's by foreign intelligence chief Rustem Umerov, with presidential office chief Kyrylo Budanov also taking part. Ukrainian negotiators spent roughly two months preparing, Umerov said, and Kyiv's mandate covers "all the issues", with security guarantees the priority.
What each side argues is now on the record, and the two positions pull in opposite directions. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said after the day's session that Russia would not agree to an immediate ceasefire without knowing what would happen next — in Moscow's telling, the outlines of a future European security architecture should be agreed first, and only then should the fighting stop. Kyiv and its European backers want the reverse: Ukraine is seeking binding assurances that Russia will not invade again and wants the fighting to stop, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Monday that any meaningful discussion of Europe's security architecture can only come once a ceasefire is achieved. On territory, Moscow wants Ukraine to withdraw from the parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson that it claims to have annexed; Kyiv refuses to cede territory and has proposed freezing the conflict along the current front line. US officials have said both sides showed "a little bit of flexibility" in private, but neither government has said anything similar in public, and President Trump has publicly suggested Ukraine will end up with "a little bit different shape" — a remark Kyiv has not welcomed.
Europe's place at the table was contested all week. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov insisted the format is strictly three-way, and Kushner described the Europeans as being kept informed on the sidelines, with a wider format only after progress is made. Even so, European officials from the UK, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission met the US and Ukrainian teams in Abu Dhabi, and a joint statement said any settlement must respect Ukraine's sovereignty, territorial integrity and independent decision-making, and that a strong NATO will continue to be central to collective Euro-Atlantic security. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Europe does not need to establish a new security architecture.
For ordinary Ukrainians, the overnight strikes are the point, not the talks. The grid attacks are part of a renewed air campaign as winter approaches, and Moscow has expanded its targeting in recent months to businesses, consumer logistics and other economic targets — a home improvement store in Kirovohrad was hit overnight — in a bid to weaken the war effort. Homes across six regions woke up without power, and Ukraine has struggled to intercept the fast-moving ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones. One small humanitarian step stands out against that: a six-day local ceasefire around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky at the end of October and beginning of November allowed civilians to leave and aid to get in, and the US says it will keep working on prisoner exchanges and other humanitarian issues.
In short: the first three-way talks in nine months opened in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and ended day one with the same split — Moscow wants a security order agreed before a ceasefire, Kyiv wants the ceasefire first, and neither side has budged on territory — while Russia kept hitting Ukraine's power grid overnight, killing two people and cutting power in six regions. The second session is Wednesday, and Washington has signalled it may follow Abu Dhabi with separate meetings with Putin and Zelensky.
Sources:
Source: tbsnews.net.

item.title: Houthis/Saudi — overnight update: drone downed over Eastern Province, Saudi jets hit Sanaa
item.description:
The overnight exchange covered in the night brief — three Houthi missiles intercepted, two aimed at Riyadh and one at the south — had two additions on Tuesday morning.
The coalition later said it also intercepted and destroyed a drone over Saudi Arabia's oil-rich Eastern Province, and the Houthi-run Saba news agency reported Saudi airstrikes on Sanaa, hitting the al-Mufazir gas station in the Jadar district north of the capital and a building belonging to the state oil company in southern Sanaa. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the Sanaa strikes, and the Houthis did not immediately claim the overnight launches.
No casualties were reported from the interceptions. (Reuters via RadioCMS)
Source: 1502-6478b717a4a2f.radiocms.com.

item.title: Iran — Canada reimposes sanctions; US answer still due today
item.description:
Canada reimposed sanctions on 11 Iranian entities on Tuesday for contributing to Iran's nuclear activities and ballistic missile programme, Foreign Minister Anita Anand said.
The list includes Iran's Nuclear Fuel Production and Procurement Company, the Nuclear Reactors Fuel Company, the National Iranian Oil Company and the National Iranian Tanker Company. The US answer to Tehran's two-day Hormuz proposal is still expected today, with Qatari officials due in Tehran the same day.
Iran has not responded to the single-source report of a phased US offer (partial blockade lift first, then nuclear talks), and Tehran's own officials remain split — Pezeshkian talking negotiation, security chief Rezaei calling talk of a deal "fake news". (Reuters)
Source: reuters.com.
